title: Lecture 6: Continuous distributions and the normal model
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question.
Start with the prediction from your prep. For a continuous random variable,
\[P(X=x)=0 \quad\text{for every single value } x.\]
Not very small — exactly zero. An interval contains infinitely many values; if each single value carried even the tiniest positive probability, the total would exceed 1. Yet the negotiation certainly takes some amount of time, so probability has not disappeared. It has moved: probability now belongs to intervals, not points. That forces a new object to replace the PMF, and building that object is the first job of this lecture.

From probability mass to probability density

MIT explanation (review): 08.2 Probability Density Functions.

For a discrete random variable, the PMF assigns probability to individual values. For a continuous random variable \(X\), a probability density function (PDF), written \(f_X(x)\), is a non-negative curve whose total area is 1. The probability that \(X\) lies between \(a\) and \(b\) is the area under the curve between those values.
You do not need calculus in this course. You need to interpret probability as area and use a CDF, R, or supplied values to calculate it.
The crucial reading rule: density is height, probability is area. Density is probability per unit of \(x\) — roughly, the probability of a tiny interval divided by its width. Because a width can be small, the height can be large. A density can exceed 1 as long as the total area under the curve is 1.






Check: is a rectangle of width 0.5 and height 2 a valid density?





Yes. The curve is non-negative and its total area is \(0.5 \times 2 = 1\), so it is a legitimate PDF (a uniform density on an interval of length 0.5). The height 2 is not a probability — no probability statement here exceeds 1, because every probability is an area inside that rectangle. Height 2 simply means the probability is packed into a narrow range.




The CDF works for every random variable
The cumulative distribution function is still
\[F_X(x)=P(X\le x),\]
exactly as in Lecture 3. For a continuous random variable,
\[P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a).\]
Because a single point has zero probability, changing \(<\) to \(\le\) does not change a continuous probability: \(P(a<X<b)\), \(P(a\le X\le b)\), and the two mixed versions are all equal. This differs from a discrete variable, where a point may carry positive probability and the inequality type matters.



The uniform distribution

MIT explanation (review): 05.5 Uniform Random Variables.

If every equal-length subinterval of \([a,b]\) is equally likely, then \(X\sim U(a,b)\). Its density is constant:
\[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{b-a},\qquad a\le x\le b,\]
and zero outside the support \([a,b]\). The height is not a choice — it is forced by the requirement that the whole rectangle have area 1:
\[\text{width}\times\text{height}=(b-a)\times\frac{1}{b-a}=1.\]
Because the height is constant, interval probability depends only on interval length. For \(a\le c<d\le b\),
\[P(c<X<d)=\frac{d-c}{b-a}.\]
The mean and variance are stated here without derivation:
\[E[X]=\frac{a+b}{2},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}.\]

Example 8.1 (Worked example: when does the pitch appear?) A recording session lasts 90 minutes, and an anonymised pitch is equally likely to start at any moment of it. Model the start time as \(X\sim U(0,90)\), measured in minutes.
Step 1: the height. The density is \(1/(90-0)=1/90\approx 0.011\) per minute — forced by total area 1, not chosen.
Step 2: the event. “The pitch starts during the 18-minute window from minute 30 to minute 48” is the event \(30<X<48\).
Step 3: the area. The probability is the area of the shaded rectangle in Figure 8.1:
\[P(30<X<48)=\frac{48-30}{90-0}=\frac{18}{90}=0.20.\]
For a uniform model, only the length of the window matters — any 18-minute window inside the session has probability 0.20.



See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

a <- 0
b <- 90
c_cut <- 30
d_cut <- 48
density_height <- 1 / (b - a)

support_rect <- data.frame(x = c(a, b), y = density_height)
window_rect  <- data.frame(x = c(c_cut, d_cut), y = density_height)
density_line <- data.frame(x = c(-9, a, a, b, b, 99),
                           y = c(0, 0, density_height, density_height, 0, 0))

ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = support_rect, aes(x, y), fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_area(data = window_rect, aes(x, y), fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = density_line, aes(x, y), colour = "#17324D",
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 66, y = 0.0127,
           label = "density = 1/(b - a) = 1/90",
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("segment", x = 39, xend = 39, y = 0.0042, yend = 0.0010,
           colour = "#17324D",
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "inches"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 39, y = 0.0052,
           label = "area = P(30 < X < 48) = 0.20",
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(a, c_cut, d_cut, b),
                     labels = c("a = 0", "c = 30", "d = 48", "b = 90"),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, density_height),
                     labels = c("0", "1/90"),
                     limits = c(0, 0.0145),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Minutes into the session", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 8.1: The uniform density for a pitch start time over a 90-minute session. The navy line is the density; the shaded green area is the probability of the 18-minute window, 18/90 = 0.20.





Read the horizontal axis as possible start times and the vertical axis as density, not probability. The navy density line is at 0 before minute 0, jumps to \(1/90\) on the support, and drops back to 0 after minute 90. The green probability is an area: \(18\times(1/90)=0.20\). Note the contrast with the check above — here the height is far below 1, there it was 2; both are legitimate, because only the area is a probability.






Try it: the final stretch of the session





In class this is the pair task. Same model, \(X\sim U(0,90)\). What is the probability that the pitch starts in the final 27 minutes of the session?
Step 1 (given). The event is \(63<X<90\), an interval of length \(90-63=27\) minutes inside the support.
Step 2 (you). Divide the interval length by the support length.
Step 3 (you). Interpret the result in one sentence.






Check your answer





\(P(63<X<90)=27/90=0.30\): under the uniform model there is a 30% chance the pitch starts in the final 27 minutes — larger than the 0.20 above only because the window is longer.








The normal distribution

MIT explanation (review): 08.8 Normal Random Variables.

A normal random variable is written
\[X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).\]
Read the notation carefully: the second parameter is the variance \(\sigma^2\), not the standard deviation. The density is symmetric and bell-shaped. The parameter \(\mu\) locates its centre; \(\sigma>0\) controls its spread:
\[E[X]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.\]


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

normal_curve <- data.frame(z = seq(-3.6, 3.6, length.out = 800))
normal_curve$density <- dnorm(normal_curve$z)

ggplot(normal_curve, aes(z, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(normal_curve, z >= -1 & z <= 1),
            fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#C98B2E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.16, label = "about 68%",
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.15, y = 0.425, label = "mean~mu", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2),
                     labels = expression(mu - 2 * sigma, mu - sigma, mu,
                                         mu + sigma, mu + 2 * sigma)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.43),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Value of X", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 8.2: The normal density. The shaded central area between the two grey dashed lines runs from one standard deviation below the mean to one above and contains about 68% of the distribution; the gold dashed line marks the mean μ.





The horizontal axis locates possible values relative to \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\); the vertical axis is density, and probability is again area. In the normal model, about 68% of the distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within 1.96 standard deviations. These are facts about the mathematical model — the caveat box below explains why they are not automatic facts about every dataset.

Standardising: every normal question becomes a Z question
If \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then
\[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1).\]
A z-score reports how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean. Standardising matters because the closed-book exam supplies a handful of standard-normal probabilities on the page — your job is to translate the business question into a \(Z\) question that those supplied values can answer. The hand calculation is the primary route; R only verifies it.

Example 8.2 (Worked example: normal probabilities from supplied Z values) Processing time \(Y\) (in minutes) is modelled as \(Y\sim N(50,100)\). The variance is 100, so \(\sigma=\sqrt{100}=10\). The following standard-normal probabilities are supplied, exactly as on the exam paper:
P(Z <=  1.5) = 0.9332
P(Z <=  1.0) = 0.8413
P(Z <= -1.0) = 0.1587
(a) \(P(Y\le 65)\). Standardise the boundary:
\[z=\frac{65-50}{10}=1.5,\]
so
\[P(Y\le 65)=P(Z\le 1.5)=0.9332.\]
(b) \(P(40<Y<60)\). Standardise both boundaries:
\[z_{\text{low}}=\frac{40-50}{10}=-1.0,\qquad
z_{\text{high}}=\frac{60-50}{10}=1.0,\]
then take the difference of the two cumulative probabilities, exactly as with any CDF:
\[P(40<Y<60)=P(Z\le 1.0)-P(Z\le -1.0)=0.8413-0.1587=0.6826.\]
That is the 68% rule seen in Figure 8.2: the interval runs from one standard deviation below the mean to one above.

In class the same two numbers are then produced live in R. pnorm() is the normal CDF; give it the boundary, the mean, and the standard deviation (not the variance):

pnorm(65, mean = 50, sd = 10)

[1] 0.9331928

pnorm(60, mean = 50, sd = 10) - pnorm(40, mean = 50, sd = 10)

[1] 0.6826895


The hand path and pnorm() agree. On the exam you will have the supplied values, not R, so practise the hand path first and use R to check.


The reverse direction: from percentile to raw value
pnorm() turns a value into a cumulative probability. The reverse question — which value has a given proportion below it — is answered by inverting the standardisation:
\[x=\mu+z\sigma,\]
where \(z\) is the standard-normal quantile for the chosen proportion.

Example 8.3 (Worked example: the 90th percentile of processing time) For \(Y\sim N(50,100)\), which processing time is exceeded by only 10% of cases? The supplied standard-normal quantile is \(z_{0.90}=1.2816\).
Step 1. The 90th percentile of \(Z\) is 1.2816: it lies 1.2816 standard deviations above the mean.
Step 2. Translate back to the scale of \(Y\):
\[x=\mu+z\sigma=50+1.2816\times 10=62.8 \text{ minutes.}\]
Step 3. Verify with qnorm(), the inverse of pnorm():

qnorm(0.90, mean = 50, sd = 10)

[1] 62.81552


About 62.8 minutes — 90% of processing times fall at or below it, 10% above.

The same function confirms the 1.96 in the 95% rule: the central 95% of the standard normal runs between

qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975))

[1] -1.959964  1.959964


Lectures 8 and 9 use exactly these two numbers to build confidence intervals.



Checking the normal model against data
The normal distribution is a model, not a label that every quantitative variable automatically deserves. Skewness, bounds, extreme outliers, or a few heavily repeated values can make it a poor description. The check is visual: draw the histogram of the data, overlay the normal curve with the same mean and standard deviation, and see whether the curve reproduces the bars.

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
c(mean_equity = mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct),
  sd_equity   = sd(sharks$equity_offered_pct))

mean_equity   sd_equity 
  13.207613    8.444355 




See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mean_equity <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
sd_equity <- sd(sharks$equity_offered_pct)

ggplot(sharks, aes(equity_offered_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 5),
                 fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                args = list(mean = mean_equity, sd = sd_equity),
                colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 42, y = 0.062, label = "observed pitches",
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 42, y = 0.054,
           label = "normal curve with the same mean and SD",
           colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Equity initially offered (%)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 8.3: Initial equity offered across all 1,441 recorded pitches (green bars), with the normal density that has the same mean and standard deviation (orange curve). The curve misses the skew, the bounds, and the spikes at round percentages.





Read Figure 8.3 with the five-step sequence from Lecture 1. Axes: initial equity in percentage points against density, so bar areas, not heights alone, represent proportions of pitches. Elements: green bars are the 1,441 observed offers; the orange curve is \(N(13.2,\,8.4^2)\), the normal model with the matching mean and SD. Pattern: the bars pile up between 5% and 20% and stretch out a long right tail. Deviations: the data are bounded between 0% and 100%, strongly right-skewed, and spiked at round values such as 10% and 20%; the symmetric curve puts visible probability below 0% and misses the spikes entirely. Meaning: the normal model fails for individual equity offers. A model is a choice, and this check rejects the choice.
That failure is not the end of the normal distribution’s usefulness — almost the opposite. From Lecture 8 onwards the normal model returns to describe sampling distributions of averages, and it will fit those well even though the underlying variable is as skewed as this one. That result is the central limit theorem, and it is the reason the normal model earns its central place in statistics.


Quantiles of a model distribution
A quantile of a distribution is the boundary value below which a chosen proportion of the probability lies. You already computed quantiles of data in Lectures 1 and 2 (quartiles, the median, the IQR of the equity offers). The same idea applies to a model distribution, and the reverse calculation above is exactly this: a quantile question.

Uniform: by symmetry, the median of \(U(a,b)\) is the midpoint \((a+b)/2\). For the session-timing model \(U(0,90)\), the median start time is 45 minutes — half the probability lies on each side.
Normal: quartiles sit \(0.6745\) standard deviations either side of the mean, \(\mu\pm 0.6745\sigma\). For \(Y\sim N(50,100)\):


qnorm(c(0.25, 0.75), mean = 50, sd = 10)

[1] 43.2551 56.7449


So the middle half of the model distribution runs from about 43.3 to 56.7 minutes. Nothing more is needed here: quantiles of data were covered earlier in the course, and quantiles of models are one qnorm() or one midpoint away.

What a normal label can and cannot say
“\(X\) is normally distributed” is a model claim, not a fact about every variable — it must be checked, the way Figure 8.3 checked it and found it false for equity offers. The 68% and 95% rules are exact statements about the mathematical normal model; quoting them for a variable that is skewed, bounded, or spiked (most business variables are at least one of these) produces confident-sounding numbers that are simply wrong. Model probabilities such as \(P(Y\le 65)=0.9332\) are conclusions inside the model \(N(50,100)\); they say nothing about reality unless the model describes the data. And a fitted curve that matches the mean and SD of the data can still miss the shape entirely — matching two summaries is not a fit. The legitimate uses ahead: the normal as a checked model for some variables, and — from Lecture 8 — as the reliable model for sampling distributions of averages, where mathematics rather than wishful thinking puts it there.



Answering the driving question
No single negotiation time or invested amount has positive probability — \(P(X=x)=0\) — so probabilities are assigned to intervals as areas under a density. For the uniform session model, the 18-minute window gets \(18/90=0.20\) because only length matters. For the normal processing-time model \(N(50,100)\), supplied \(Z\) values give \(P(Y\le 65)=0.9332\) and \(P(40<Y<60)=0.6826\) by hand, and pnorm() confirms both. The catch: a density is a modelling choice, and the equity histogram shows the normal choice failing for real offers — so check the model before trusting its areas.
Next: We can now model quantities that live on a continuum and read probabilities as areas. Everything so far, though, treats the 1,441 records as the whole world — and real analysis rarely has the whole world. Firms see samples: 100 audited transactions, 500 surveyed customers. Lecture 7 makes the move from one pitch to a sample of pitches: populations, frames, and random sampling, plus the discipline of parameters, estimators, and estimates on which all of inference stands.

title: Lecture 6: Continuous distributions and the normal model
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 55 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

Why is \(P(X=x)=0\) for a continuous random variable?
What quantity under a PDF represents probability?
How do you obtain \(P(a<X\le b)\) from a CDF?
What do \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) control in a normal model?
A density curve reaches a height of 2. Why is that not a contradiction?
What does a z-score of \(-1.5\) mean?







Check your answers






Probability belongs to intervals; an individual point has zero width and therefore zero area.
Area under the density curve between the interval boundaries.
\(F_X(b)-F_X(a)\).
\(\mu\) controls the centre and \(\sigma\) the spread.
Density is probability per unit, not probability. A height above 1 is fine as long as the total area under the curve is 1.
The value lies 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.






From worked to faded (5 minutes)
Re-read the session-timing calculation (Example 8.1). Then complete the same calculation for a new model: a waiting time \(X\sim U(10,30)\) minutes.
Step 1 (given). The density height is \(1/(30-10)=0.05\) on the support \([10,30]\) and zero outside it.
Step 2 (you). Find \(P(14<X<20)\).
Step 3 (you). State \(E[X]\) and interpret both numbers in one sentence.






Check your answer





\(P(14<X<20)=(20-14)/(30-10)=6/20=0.30\) and \(E[X]=(10+30)/2=20\): the wait averages 20 minutes, and under the uniform model there is a 30% chance it lands between 14 and 20 minutes.





Practice (15 minutes)
For items 3 and 4, use only these supplied values, then verify in R:
P(Z <=  1.5) = 0.9332
P(Z <=  1.0) = 0.8413
P(Z <= -1.0) = 0.1587
z(0.90)      = 1.2816

For \(X\sim U(10,30)\): find \(\operatorname{SD}(X)\) and \(P(X>25)\).
A supplier delivers at a moment uniformly distributed between 09:00 and 13:00. Your goods lift is reserved for other tenants except during 12:00–13:00. What is the probability the delivery arrives while the lift is available, and what is the density height per minute?
Monthly demand for a product is modelled as \(Y\sim N(200,400)\). Calculate \(P(Y\le 230)\) and \(P(180<Y<220)\) by hand.
Weekly revenue is modelled as \(N(100,15^2)\) (in hundreds of euros). Which revenue level is exceeded in only 10% of weeks? Compute by hand with \(x=\mu+z\sigma\), then verify with qnorm().
Explain in two sentences why the normal curve in Figure 8.3 is not a convincing model for offered equity.







Check your answers






\(\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{(30-10)^2/12}=20/\sqrt{12}\approx 5.77\) minutes, and \(P(X>25)=(30-25)/20=0.25\).
The window is 60 of the 240 possible minutes, so \(60/240=0.25\). The density height is \(1/240\approx 0.0042\) per minute — and the probability is the area \(60\times(1/240)=0.25\), not the height.
\(\sigma=\sqrt{400}=20\). For 230: \(z=(230-200)/20=1.5\), so \(P(Y\le 230)=0.9332\). For the interval: \(z_{\text{low}}=(180-200)/20=-1.0\) and \(z_{\text{high}}=(220-200)/20=1.0\), so \(P(180<Y<220)=0.8413-0.1587=0.6826\).
\(x=100+1.2816\times 15=119.2\), so about 119 hundred euros; only 10% of weeks exceed it.
The observed distribution is bounded between 0% and 100%, strongly right-skewed, and concentrated at a few round percentages; the symmetric normal curve reproduces none of those features.

Verification in R for items 3 and 4:

pnorm(230, mean = 200, sd = 20)

[1] 0.9331928

pnorm(220, mean = 200, sd = 20) - pnorm(180, mean = 200, sd = 20)

[1] 0.6826895

qnorm(0.90, mean = 100, sd = 15)

[1] 119.2233







Spaced review: one item from Lecture 3 (5 minutes)
The number of sharks who join an on-air deal, \(X\), has PMF \(p(1)=0.6\), \(p(2)=0.3\), \(p(3)=0.1\). Find \(F(2)=P(X\le 2)\) and \(P(X<2)\). Why do the two answers differ here, when for a continuous variable they would not?






Check your answer





\(F(2)=0.6+0.3=0.9\), while \(P(X<2)=P(X=1)=0.6\). They differ because the single point \(X=2\) carries positive probability, \(p(2)=0.3\). For a continuous variable every single point has probability zero, so \(<\) and \(\le\) give the same answer.





Changing units (5 minutes)
The session-timing variable \(X\sim U(0,90)\) is recorded in minutes and then converted to seconds. Explain what changes about the PDF and what remains unchanged.






Check your answer





The support stretches from \([0,90]\) minutes to \([0,5400]\) seconds, and the density height drops from \(1/90\) per minute to \(1/5400\) per second — the numerical size of a density depends on the units. Probabilities of corresponding time intervals are unchanged, because they are areas: the 18-minute window becomes a 1,080-second window, and \(1080/5400=18/90=0.20\).





Exam-style item (10 minutes)
This item follows the pattern of Mock Exam Question 3. Let \(X\sim U(20,60)\) be a waiting time in minutes and, separately, \(Y\sim N(80,25)\) a processing time in minutes. Supplied:
P(Z <=  1.5) = 0.9332
P(Z <=  1.0) = 0.8413
P(Z <= -1.0) = 0.1587

State the PDF height of \(X\), including its value outside the support.
Calculate \(P(30<X<40)\), \(E[X]\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
Standardise 87.5 minutes under the model for \(Y\), then calculate \(P(Y\le 87.5)\).
Calculate \(P(75<Y<85)\).
Explain why a PDF height is not itself a probability.







Check a model answer






\(f_X(x)=1/(60-20)=0.025\) for \(20\le x\le 60\), and \(f_X(x)=0\) outside that interval.
\(P(30<X<40)=(40-30)/40=0.25\), \(E[X]=(20+60)/2=40\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(60-20)^2/12\approx 133.33\) square minutes.
The variance is 25, so \(\sigma=5\) and \(z=(87.5-80)/5=1.5\); hence \(P(Y\le 87.5)=0.9332\).
\(P(75<Y<85)=P(-1<Z<1)=0.8413-0.1587=0.6826\).
Probability is area over an interval — approximately density times a small interval width. A single point has zero width and hence zero probability; a density value only becomes a probability once multiplied by a width.






Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture — or any business you know well. Pick one continuous quantity that matters for it (a delivery time, weekly revenue, time on site) and write two sentences: first name the interval of values that would trigger a real decision, then say whether a uniform or a normal model seems defensible for that quantity — and which feature of its histogram you would check first. There is no wrong answer; the point is connecting today’s tools to something you care about.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “Delivery time is my quantity: anything over 40 minutes triggers a refund, so \(P(T > 40)\) is the number that matters. A normal model is doubtful because times cannot be negative and a few deliveries go very wrong — right skew is the first thing I would check on the histogram.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to propose a distribution for your quantity and then challenge whether the normal model’s assumptions actually hold for it.

Continue to Lecture 7: Samples, parameters, and estimators.
Formula sheet: Lecture 6 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapter 10.

title: Lecture 7: Samples, parameters, and estimators
text:
Before class
Total preparation time: about 25 minutes.
Reactivate (10 minutes). Suppose we want the mean initial equity offered across the 1,441 recorded pitches in completed Seasons 1–16, but can inspect only 100 randomly selected records. Identify:
Predict (5 minutes). Answer the one-click Mentimeter question posted on Canvas before you come to class: two students each draw their own random sample of 100 pitches from the file and each compute the mean equity offered. Will their two sample means be equal? Commit to an answer; the lecture resolves it.
If subscripts or summation notation are not secure, review Mathematics Refresher: indices and sums.

title: Lecture 7: Samples, parameters, and estimators
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Your prep prediction — do two random samples give equal means? — stays on screen, unresolved, until the sampling activity below settles it with evidence.

Define the population before calculating
A population is the complete set of units about which a question is asked. A sample is the subset observed for analysis. A sampling frame is the list or mechanism from which the sample is selected. The target population is the broader group to which we hope to generalise.
These sets need not coincide. The teaching file is a near-census of recorded US Shark Tank pitches from completed Seasons 1–16, but it is not a random sample of all entrepreneurs, all funding pitches, or even all applicants to the show. Randomly sampling rows from this file supports inference to the 1,441-record population. It does not remove the show’s selection process.






Check: classify two scenarios





Scenario A. A food-delivery startup wants to know how satisfied “its customers” are. It emails a survey to the app users who opted in to marketing emails; 800 reply. Identify the target population, the frame, and the sample.
Scenario B. A consultant uses our 100 sampled pitches to advise “US entrepreneurs seeking investors.” What is the frame, and what is the target population being claimed?
Answers. In A, the target population is all customers; the frame is the opted-in email list (which already excludes many customers); the sample is the 800 who chose to reply — a voluntary-response subset of an incomplete frame. In B, the frame is the 1,441 recorded Shark Tank pitches; the claimed target population is all US entrepreneurs seeking investors. Random row sampling licenses conclusions about the frame, not about that far larger target group.





Simple random sampling
In a simple random sample of size \(n\), every set of \(n\) population units has the same chance of selection.

With replacement: a selected unit is returned before the next draw. Draws are independent and each draw has the same distribution.
Without replacement: a unit cannot be selected twice. Draws are dependent, although every draw has the same marginal distribution.

When a without-replacement sample is a small fraction of a large population, the dependence is weak. This course uses the 10% condition as a practical working rule: if \(n\le 0.10N\), the usual independent-sample standard-error formulas are a good approximation.
The running sample for this lecture and the next is drawn with a visible seed, so every reader gets the same 100 rows:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

nrow(pitch_sample)

[1] 100


Here \(100/1441\approx 0.069<0.10\), so the working rule is satisfied.
How does this one realised sample compare to the population it came from?


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

breaks <- seq(0, 100, by = 5)
pop_hist <- hist(sharks$equity_offered_pct, breaks = breaks, plot = FALSE)
samp_hist <- hist(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, breaks = breaks,
                  plot = FALSE)
pop_density <- data.frame(mid = pop_hist$mids, density = pop_hist$density)
samp_density <- data.frame(mid = samp_hist$mids, density = samp_hist$density)

ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = pop_density, aes(mid, density), width = 5,
           fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_line(data = samp_density, aes(mid, density),
            colour = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = samp_density, aes(mid, density),
             colour = "#009E73", size = 2.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 40, y = 0.070, label = "all 1,441 records",
           colour = "#5B6976", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 40, y = 0.062, label = "random sample of 100",
           colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Equity initially offered (%)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 9.1: Initial equity offered: all 1,441 records (grey bars) and the seed-123 random sample of 100 (green connected points). The sample resembles the population but does not reproduce it exactly.





The horizontal axis gives equity intervals in percentage points; the vertical axis is density, so the differently sized datasets can be compared by shape. The sample resembles the population but does not reproduce it exactly — and a different random sample would resemble it differently. That observation is worth turning into an experiment.


The live sampling activity: watching an estimator vary
In class this segment runs live. The whole class watches five different random samples being drawn, one after another, and tracks one number per sample: the mean equity offered. The target of the exercise is the population mean of the file,

mu_equity <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
mu_equity

[1] 13.20761


about 13.21 percentage points — knowable here only because we happen to hold the full file. In a real study you would hold only the sample, which is exactly why the behaviour of the sample mean matters.
Five samples of 100, each from its own seed, each summarised by its mean. The code is fully reproducible — run it yourself and you will get the same five numbers:

seeds <- 101:105
sample_means <- numeric(length(seeds))
for (i in seq_along(seeds)) {
  set.seed(seeds[i])
  rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
  sample_means[i] <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct[rows])
}
round(sample_means, 2)

[1] 12.03 12.77 13.75 12.07 13.58


Five samples, five different means — from about 12.0 to about 13.8. Figure 9.2 puts them on one fixed axis, with the population mean drawn as a vertical line that never moves.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mu_equity <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)

seeds <- 101:105
sample_means <- numeric(length(seeds))
for (i in seq_along(seeds)) {
  set.seed(seeds[i])
  rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
  sample_means[i] <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct[rows])
}
five_means <- data.frame(draw = seq_along(seeds),
                         seed = paste("seed", seeds),
                         sample_mean = sample_means)

ggplot(five_means, aes(sample_mean, draw)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_equity, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#C98B2E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = "#009E73", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = mu_equity + 0.12, y = length(seeds) + 0.45,
           label = "mu == 13.21", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = five_means$draw, labels = five_means$seed) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 16),
                  ylim = c(0.5, length(seeds) + 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean equity offered (%)", y = "Draw") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 9.2: Five random samples of 100, five sample means (green dots), one fixed population mean (gold dashed line at 13.21). The estimate varies from draw to draw; the parameter sits still.





Read the figure slowly, because Lecture 8 is built on it. Each green dot is one estimate: the realised mean of one realised sample. The gold dashed line is the parameter: one fixed, unmoving number. The dots scatter around the line — none hits it exactly, none is far from it, and no dot is “wrong.” The scatter is not a mistake in the procedure; it is the procedure. Random samples produce random estimates.
This resolves the prep prediction: two students drawing their own random samples will almost never get equal means. Any two of the five dots differ, and yours (in the after-class task below) will differ again.
In class the five-dot plot stays on screen through the break, with one question to chew on: if we drew a sixth sample, where would its mean land? You cannot say exactly — but by now you can say something about the range in which it would probably fall. Making that “something” precise is the entire subject of Lecture 8.


Parameters, estimators, and estimates

MIT explanation (review): 20.3 The Sample Mean and Some Terminology.

A parameter is a fixed numerical property of a population, usually unknown. An estimator is a rule based on random sample variables. Its value changes from sample to sample. An estimate is the number obtained from one realised sample.
For a random sample \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\):
\[\bar X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\]
is an estimator of the population mean \(\mu\). After observing values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\),
\[\bar x=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\]
is the realised estimate. Capital letters describe random quantities before sampling; lower-case letters describe observed values.
For a 0/1 variable, the sample proportion is a sample mean:
\[\widehat P=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.\]
Its realised value is written \(\hat p\).
The usual sample variance and standard deviation are
\[S^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i-\bar X)^2,
\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.\]
The denominator \(n-1\) makes \(S^2\) an unbiased estimator of population variance under independent random sampling.
The realised estimates for our seed-123 sample:

c(
  sample_mean_equity = mean(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sample_sd_equity = sd(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sample_deal_proportion = mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)
)

    sample_mean_equity       sample_sd_equity sample_deal_proportion 
             12.760000               7.707887               0.640000 


For this realised sample, \(\bar x=12.76\) percentage points, \(s=7.71\) percentage points, and \(\hat p=0.64\).

Example 9.1 (Worked example: three objects for the deal proportion) Identify the parameter, the estimator, and the estimate for the proportion of deals, using our realised sample.

Parameter: \(p\), the proportion of the 1,441 records with an on-air deal — one fixed number. Because the file is a near-census of its frame, we can even look it up: \(882/1441\approx 0.612\). In a real study it would be unknown.
Estimator: \(\widehat P=\frac{1}{100}\sum_{i=1}^{100}X_i\), where \(X_i\) is the deal indicator of the \(i\)-th sampled record — a rule whose value is random because the sample is.
Estimate: \(\hat p=0.64\), the number the rule produced for the seed-123 sample. A different seed would produce a different \(\hat p\) while \(p\) stayed exactly where it was.




Why the sample variance has \(n-1\) degrees of freedom
Once \(\bar X\) has been calculated from the same sample, the deviations must satisfy
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i-\bar X)=0.\]
If \(n-1\) deviations are known, the final deviation is forced to make the sum zero. Only \(n-1\) deviations can vary freely: the sample variance has \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.

Example 9.2 (Worked example: three deviations, two degrees of freedom) Suppose a sample has \(n=3\) observations and the first two deviations from the sample mean are \(2\) and \(-5\).
Step 1. The deviations must sum to zero: \(2+(-5)+d_3=0\).
Step 2. Solve: \(d_3=3\). The third deviation cannot be chosen freely — it is forced.
Step 3. Count the freedom: three deviations, but only two carried any information once the sample mean was fixed. The sample variance for this sample has \(3-1=2\) degrees of freedom.

Using the fitted sample mean makes squared deviations around \(\bar X\) slightly too small on average as a measure of population spread. Dividing by \(n-1\), rather than \(n\), corrects that downward bias under the random-sample model. Degrees of freedom count remaining independent pieces of information; they are not a percentage or a probability.


Sampling method determines the evidence boundary
The number of rows does not identify the sampling design. Ask how units entered the data:








Method
How units enter
Main implication




Simple random sample
selected by a known random mechanism
supports design-based generalisation to the frame


Stratified random sample
randomly selected within defined groups
can guarantee representation of important groups


Convenience sample
selected because they are easy to reach
vulnerable to selection bias


Voluntary-response sample
units choose whether to respond
people with stronger views may be over-represented


Census of a frame
every unit in the available frame is recorded
no sampling error for that frame, but coverage error can remain



The Shark Tank teaching file is close to a census of its recorded-pitch frame. When we draw 100 rows for an inference exercise, the randomisation is created by our row-sampling procedure. It does not make the television programme’s selection of pitches random.






Try it: classify four recruitment stories





In class this is the pair task. For each story, name the sampling method from the table and state its main threat.
Story 1 (given, as a model). “A ministry lists all registered firms, groups them by province, and randomly selects firms within each province.” Method: stratified random sample. Main implication: representation of every province is guaranteed by design.
Story 2 (you). “A startup posts a poll on its own Instagram account asking followers to rate a prototype; 412 followers respond.”
Story 3 (you). “A student emails the survey to friends, family, and two student associations she belongs to.”
Story 4 (you). “A researcher numbers all 8,214 firms in the Chamber of Commerce register and selects 300 using a random number generator.”






Check your answer





Story 2: voluntary-response sample — followers already like the brand, and those with the strongest opinions are most likely to reply. Story 3: convenience sample — easy-to-reach contacts are systematically unlike the wider population, so selection bias is the main threat. Story 4: simple random sample from the register — it supports generalisation to the registered-firm frame, though firms missing from the register remain out of reach (coverage error).






Random selection reduces systematic over-representation within the sampling frame. It does not guarantee that one realised sample is perfectly balanced: by chance, a sample can contain unusually many large equity offers or unusually many deals. Larger samples reduce this random instability — the five-dot plot would tighten if each dot summarised 1,000 draws instead of 100.

What random selection can and cannot repair
Random sampling supports generalisation from the sample to the frame it was drawn from: our 100 rows speak, with quantifiable uncertainty, for the 1,441 recorded pitches. Random assignment — allocating units to treatments by chance — supports causal comparison. They answer different design questions and neither substitutes for the other. And neither repairs the show’s selection: the frame itself was assembled by producers choosing telegenic pitches, so no amount of careful random row-sampling turns conclusions about this file into conclusions about entrepreneurs in general. Finally, “unbiased” is a promise about the procedure across many samples, not about your one realised estimate: \(\bar x = 12.76\) is not \(\mu = 13.21\), and no single sample can tell you how far off it is.



Answering the driving question
One hundred randomly chosen records give estimates of the file’s parameters: the seed-123 sample estimates the mean equity offer at \(\bar x=12.76\) against the true \(\mu=13.21\), and the deal proportion at \(\hat p=0.64\) against \(p\approx 0.612\). Five repeated draws put the sample mean between about 12.0 and 13.8 while the parameter never moved — random samples inform us about the frame, with a random error whose size Lecture 8 will quantify. What they can never tell us: anything reliable about entrepreneurs in general, because the frame is a television programme’s curated selection, and our row-sampling randomness cannot undo that.
Next: We now speak carefully about samples: the parameter sits still while the estimator varies from sample to sample — you watched five sample means land in five different places. Lecture 8 studies the pattern behind those dots: the sampling distribution of the mean, the standard error that measures its spread, and the central limit theorem, which explains why averages turn bell-shaped even when the underlying data are wildly skewed. That pattern is what will let us attach a margin of error to any estimate.

title: Lecture 7: Samples, parameters, and estimators
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 50 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

What is the difference between a target population and a sampling frame?
Why are draws without replacement dependent?
What is the difference between an estimator and an estimate?
Why is a sample proportion a sample mean?
Why does the sample variance have \(n-1\) degrees of freedom?
What does random sampling support that random assignment does not?







Check your answers






The target population is the group of substantive interest; the sampling frame is the set from which units can actually be selected.
Selecting one unit changes which units remain available.
An estimator is a random rule before data are observed; an estimate is its realised numerical value.
A 0/1 indicator sums to the number of successes, so its mean is the success proportion.
Estimating the sample mean imposes one constraint: all deviations from it must sum to zero. Only \(n-1\) deviations can vary freely.
Random sampling supports generalisation to the sampling frame; random assignment supports causal comparison of treatments.






Practice (15 minutes)

For a population of \(N=20{,}000\) customers and a simple random sample of \(n=500\), check the 10% condition.
Write the estimator and realised estimate for the population deal proportion.
Explain why \(\mu\) is fixed while \(\bar X\) is random.
Using pitch_sample, calculate the sample mean and sample SD of description_words.
Explain why this random sample cannot justify conclusions about all US entrepreneurs.
For a sample of five observations, state the degrees of freedom used to estimate variance and explain the number.







Check your answers






\(500/20{,}000=0.025<0.10\), so the condition is satisfied.
The estimator is \(\widehat P=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i\); the realised estimate is \(\hat p=n^{-1}\sum_ix_i\) — here \(0.64\).
The population and its mean are treated as fixed; the selected observations, and therefore their mean, vary across possible samples.
Rebuild the sample and compute — about 4.82 words with an SD of about 1.76:


sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]
c(mean = mean(pitch_sample$description_words),
  sd   = sd(pitch_sample$description_words))

   mean      sd 
4.82000 1.76028 



The sample was selected from televised records, not from all US entrepreneurs; random row selection cannot repair that coverage gap.
The degrees of freedom are \(5-1=4\). Once the sample mean is estimated, four deviations may vary freely and the fifth is fixed by their zero sum.






Draw your own sample (10 minutes)
Add a dot of your own to the class version of Figure 9.2. Use your student number as the seed, draw your own sample of 100, and compute your mean equity offer:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
my_seed <- 2412345   # replace with your own student number
set.seed(my_seed)
rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct[rows])

Submit your mean to the shared class plot on Canvas (the Mentimeter link is posted under Lecture 7). Every student uses a different seed, so every student contributes a different dot.






Check: what will the class plot show?





Two hundred dots will not scatter arbitrarily: they will pile up around 13.2, thin out towards the edges, and form a recognisable shape. That shape — the sampling distribution of the mean — is exactly what Lecture 8 names, describes, and puts to work.





Spaced review: one item from Lecture 6 (5 minutes)
Processing time is modelled as \(Y\sim N(50,100)\), and \(P(Z\le 1.5)=0.9332\) is supplied. Find \(P(Y>65)\) by hand.






Check your answer





\(\sigma=\sqrt{100}=10\) and \(z=(65-50)/10=1.5\), so \(P(Y>65)=1-P(Z\le 1.5)=1-0.9332=0.0668\): under this model, about 6.7% of processing times exceed 65 minutes.





Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question. A retailer’s loyalty programme has 52,000 members. An analyst draws 400 members at random; their mean January spend is €87.40. A slide then claims: “the average member spends €87.40 per month.” Identify the parameter, the estimator, and the estimate, and give two distinct objections to the claim.






Check a model answer





The parameter is the mean January spend across all 52,000 members (fixed, unknown). The estimator is the sample mean \(\bar X\) of 400 randomly drawn members’ spends. The estimate is \(\bar x=87.40\) euros. Objections: first, the estimate carries sampling error — another random 400 members would give a different mean, so €87.40 should be reported with its uncertainty (Lectures 8–9); second, the claim generalises a January figure to “per month,” which the data cannot support — the frame covers one month’s spending only.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture — or any business you know well. Write two sentences: first name one group you would genuinely want to learn about (your target population) and the best list of its members you could actually get your hands on (your frame), then say where the gap between the two would bite if you sampled from that list. There is no wrong answer; the point is connecting today’s tools to something you care about.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “I want to learn about all students on campus who buy lunch at least twice a week, but the best list I can actually get is my own mailing list. Sampling from that list overrepresents existing fans, so any satisfaction estimate would be too rosy for the market I want to enter next.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to hunt for coverage gaps in your frame and to suggest who your sample would silently leave out.

Continue to Lecture 8: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem.
Formula sheet: Lecture 7 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapter 12.

title: Lecture 8: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
Before class
Total preparation time: about 30 minutes.
Reactivate (10 minutes). Classify each object as a population distribution, a sampling distribution, or a realised estimate:
Predict (5 minutes). Answer the one-click Mentimeter question posted on Canvas before you come to class: to cut the typical error of a sample mean in half, do you need \(2\times\), \(4\times\), or \(10\times\) the observations? Commit to an answer; the lecture resolves it.

title: Lecture 8: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Start from where Lecture 7 ended: the five dots. Five random samples of 100 pitches produced five different sample means, plotted on one axis, while the population mean sat still underneath them. During the break you guessed where a sixth mean would land. This lecture is about the pattern behind those dots — the hardest and most useful idea in the course.

The pattern behind the five dots
Imagine not five samples but every possible random sample of the same size, each producing its own sample mean. The distribution of those possible values of \(\bar X\) is its sampling distribution. It describes uncertainty in an estimator, not variation among individual pitches:

the population distribution describes how equity offers vary across the 1,441 pitches;
the sampling distribution describes how \(\bar X\) would vary across repeated samples;
a realised estimate, such as 12.76, is one draw from that sampling distribution.

The two population parameters this chapter keeps returning to are the frame mean and SD of equity offered, and the frame deal proportion. Construct them yourself — because the 1,441 records are the entire frame, the SD divides by \(N\), not \(n-1\):

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mu_equity <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
sigma_equity <- sqrt(mean((sharks$equity_offered_pct - mu_equity)^2))
p_deal <- mean(sharks$deal_on_show)
c(mu_equity = mu_equity, sigma_equity = sigma_equity, p_deal = p_deal)

   mu_equity sigma_equity       p_deal 
  13.2076128    8.4414247    0.6120749 


So \(\mu = 13.21\) percentage points, \(\sigma = 8.44\) percentage points, and \(p = 0.612\). These are fixed numbers. What varies is any statistic computed from a random sample of the frame.


Explore it: the sampling-distribution lab
Before any formula, see the sampling distribution form. The lab below shows the strongly right-skewed population histogram of the 1,441 equity offers on the left. Use the slider to choose a sample size \(n\) and press Redraw to draw many random samples of that size: each sample’s mean drops into the histogram forming on the right, next to the population.


Work through three settings and watch three things — centre, spread, shape:

Set \(n = 2\) and redraw several times. The means scatter widely and the histogram of means is still skewed.
Set \(n = 25\). The histogram of means narrows and starts to look symmetric, centred near 13.2.
Slide up to \(n = 100\). The histogram of means is a tight, bell-shaped pile around the population mean, even though the population histogram beside it has not changed at all.

Everything in the rest of this lecture is the mathematics of what you just manipulated: where the pile sits, how wide it is, and why it becomes bell-shaped.


The mean and variance of a sample mean
For independent, identically distributed variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with population mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\),
\[
E[\bar X]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},
\qquad
\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
The first equality says that \(\bar X\) is unbiased for \(\mu\): the pile of sample means is centred on the parameter, exactly as in the lab. The third quantity — the SD of the estimator across repeated samples — is called the standard error (SE). An SD describes variation among observations; an SE describes variation of an estimator.
These are not new facts. They follow from the linearity rules you already have on the formula sheet (the Lecture 8 block, and the Refresher’s linearity rules):

\(E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]\) and \(E[aX]=aE[X]\), so \(E[\bar X]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[X_i]=\frac{1}{n}\,n\mu=\mu\);
\(\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and, for independent variables, \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)\), so

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)
=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n}{n}\right)
=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)
=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
Independent positive and negative deviations partly cancel in an average. That cancellation is why the right-hand histogram in the lab is so much narrower than the population histogram.
In practice \(\sigma\) is usually unknown and is estimated by the sample SD \(S\), giving the estimated standard error \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=S/\sqrt n\). Substituting an estimate for a parameter adds a little extra uncertainty; Lecture 9 opens with the price of that substitution.

Example 10.1 (Worked example: E, Var, and SE for σ = 12, n = 36) A population has mean \(\mu\) and SD \(\sigma=12\). A random sample of \(n=36\) observations is drawn. Find the mean, variance, and SE of \(\bar X\), naming the rule used at each step.

Mean. By linearity of expectation (\(E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]\), \(E[aX]=aE[X]\)), \(E[\bar X]=\mu\) — whatever \(\mu\) is, the sample mean is unbiased for it.
Variance. By \(\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and additivity of variance under independence, \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n=12^2/36=144/36=4\).
SE. Take the square root: \(\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=\sqrt 4=2\), i.e. \(\sigma/\sqrt n=12/6=2\).

The typical distance between a sample mean and \(\mu\) is about 2 units — one sixth of the typical distance of a single observation from \(\mu\). All three rules are on the formula sheet; the derivations are in the Mathematics Refresher.



The square-root rule
Precision grows with \(\sqrt n\), not with \(n\). This resolves the prep prediction: to cut the SE in half you need \(\mathbf{4\times}\) the observations, because
\[
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{4n}}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Doubling the sample buys less than you might hope; each extra digit of precision gets more expensive. This is worth knowing before you budget for any data collection.






Try it: how large must n become to cut an SE from 4 to 1?





In class this is the pair task before the break. Complete the missing steps before opening the answer.
Step 1 (given). The SE must fall by a factor of \(4/1 = 4\).
Step 2 (you). The SE is proportional to \(1/\sqrt n\). By what factor must \(n\) change to divide the SE by 4?
Step 3 (you). If the original sample had \(n=50\), how many observations does the new design need?






Check your answer





Dividing the SE by 4 requires multiplying \(n\) by \(4^2=16\): the square-root rule in reverse. From \(n=50\) the design needs \(16\times 50=800\) observations. Precision is bought at a quadratic price.








The central limit theorem

MIT explanation (review): 19.2 The Central Limit Theorem.

The lab showed one more pattern that the mean-and-variance rules do not explain: the pile of sample means became bell-shaped, even though the population is strongly skewed. That is the central limit theorem (CLT). Under the independent-sampling conditions used in this course, the standardised sample mean
\[
Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
\]
approaches a standard normal distribution as \(n\) grows. Equivalently,
\[
\bar X\ \dot\sim\ N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
\]
for a sufficiently large sample. The dot above \(\sim\) signals an approximation. The normal model from Lecture 6 returns here — not as a model for the data, where it failed for equity offers, but as a model for the sample mean.
There is no universal rule that \(n=30\) is always enough. Strong skewness, extreme outliers, or dependence between observations may require much more data. If the population itself is normal, the sample mean is exactly normal for every \(n\).
Figure 10.1 shows the simulation behind the claim: 5,000 sample means of \(n=5\) draws and 5,000 sample means of \(n=40\) draws from the equity variable.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mu_equity <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
sigma_equity <- sqrt(mean((sharks$equity_offered_pct - mu_equity)^2))
set.seed(208)
B <- 5000
means_5 <- replicate(B, mean(sample(sharks$equity_offered_pct, 5,
                                    replace = TRUE)))
means_40 <- replicate(B, mean(sample(sharks$equity_offered_pct, 40,
                                     replace = TRUE)))

panel_levels <- c("n = 5", "n = 40")
sim_means <- data.frame(
  sample_mean = c(means_5, means_40),
  panel = factor(rep(panel_levels, each = B), levels = panel_levels)
)

all_means <- c(means_5, means_40)
shared_limits <- c(floor(min(all_means)), ceiling(max(all_means)))
shared_breaks <- seq(shared_limits[1], shared_limits[2], length.out = 36)

normal_grid <- seq(shared_limits[1], shared_limits[2], length.out = 400)
normal_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = normal_grid, panel = panel_levels[1],
             density = dnorm(normal_grid, mu_equity,
                             sigma_equity / sqrt(5))),
  data.frame(x = normal_grid, panel = panel_levels[2],
             density = dnorm(normal_grid, mu_equity,
                             sigma_equity / sqrt(40)))
)
normal_curves$panel <- factor(normal_curves$panel, levels = panel_levels)

ggplot(sim_means, aes(sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), breaks = shared_breaks,
                 fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") +
  geom_line(data = normal_curves, aes(x, density),
            colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "fixed") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean equity offered (%)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )








Figure 10.1: Simulated sampling distributions of the mean equity offered for n = 5 (left) and n = 40 (right), each based on 5,000 samples, with the corresponding normal approximations (orange curves). Both panels use the same axes.





Read Figure 10.1 with the five-step sequence. (1) Each bar counts simulated sample means, not pitches. (2) The horizontal axis is the possible sample mean of equity offered, in percentage points — the same range in both panels, so widths can be compared directly. (3) The vertical axis is density, also on a shared scale. (4) The pattern: the \(n=40\) pile is far narrower and visibly closer to its orange normal curve than the \(n=5\) pile, which still leans right like the population. (5) Takeaway: averaging 40 independent draws from a wildly skewed population already produces a concentrated, nearly normal sampling distribution.


Sample proportions are sample means
For a Bernoulli variable \(X\) with \(P(X=1)=p\) (Lecture 3),
\[
E[X]=p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p).
\]
A sample proportion is just the sample mean of an indicator, so every result above applies immediately: \(\widehat P=\bar X\) satisfies
\[
E[\widehat P]=p,
\qquad
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.
\]
Its sampling distribution is approximately normal when the expected numbers of successes and failures are both sufficiently large. This course uses \(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10\) as the working rule (the success–failure condition).

Example 10.2 (Worked example: SE of the deal proportion at n = 100) Suppose we draw a random sample of \(n=100\) pitches from the frame, where the deal proportion is \(p=0.612\). How far is the sample deal proportion typically from 0.612?

SE. \(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{0.612\,(1-0.612)/100}
=\sqrt{0.2375/100}\approx 0.0487\), about 4.9 percentage points.
Success–failure check. \(np=100(0.612)=61.2\ge 10\) and \(n(1-p)=100(0.388)=38.8\ge 10\), so the normal approximation is reasonable.

In R, using p_deal as constructed above:

p_deal <- mean(sharks$deal_on_show)
c(SE_deal_proportion_n_100 = sqrt(p_deal * (1 - p_deal) / 100),
  successes = 100 * p_deal, failures = 100 * (1 - p_deal))

SE_deal_proportion_n_100                successes                 failures 
              0.04872773              61.20749480              38.79250520 





The law of large numbers and the CLT answer different questions

MIT explanation (review): 18.4 The Weak Law of Large Numbers.


The law of large numbers (LLN) says where the pile goes: \(\bar X\) becomes close to \(\mu\) as \(n\) grows.
The CLT says what the pile looks like: the approximate shape and scale of the sampling distribution after standardisation.

One is about convergence of a value, the other about convergence of a distribution. Both assume the sampling is random; neither repairs a sample that was selected badly in the first place.






Check: match each statement to LLN, CLT, or neither






“With enough random draws, the sample mean equity will be very close to 13.21.”
“For \(n=100\) random draws, the sample mean equity is approximately \(N(13.21, 0.844^2)\).”
“With enough respondents, our LinkedIn poll will represent Dutch founders.”

Statement 1 is the LLN, statement 2 is the CLT, and statement 3 is neither: no theorem turns a self-selected sample into a representative one — see the caveat box.




What a bigger sample can and cannot fix
Everything in this lecture concerns random sampling error: the unavoidable wobble of a statistic across random samples. More observations shrink that wobble at the square-root rate. They do nothing for selection bias: if pitches enter the data because producers chose good television, a sample of a million such pitches still describes televised pitches, not entrepreneurs in general. An SE of 0.84 quantifies precision within the recorded-pitch frame; it is silent about who got into the frame, and an on-air deal is still not a completed investment.



Answering the driving question
Our sample of 100 gave mean equity 12.76, while the frame mean is 13.21. How wrong could 12.76 have been? Its standard error:

sigma_equity <- sqrt(mean((sharks$equity_offered_pct -
                             mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct))^2))
c(SE_mean_n_25 = sigma_equity / sqrt(25),
  SE_mean_n_100 = sigma_equity / sqrt(100))

 SE_mean_n_25 SE_mean_n_100 
    1.6882849     0.8441425 


At \(n=100\) the SE is about 0.84 percentage points: a random-sample mean typically lands within about 0.84 points of 13.21, and rarely more than about two SEs away. (At \(n=25\) the SE would be twice as large — the square-root rule again.) Averaging is trustworthy despite the wild skew of single pitches because deviations cancel (the variance rule) and the CLT gives the mean a predictable, nearly normal distribution.
Next: We can now say how much a sample mean typically wobbles: one standard error. Turning that into a sentence a report can carry — “the frame mean plausibly lies between \(a\) and \(b\)” — needs one more ingredient, because in a real sample the population \(\sigma\) is unknown and must be estimated too, adding uncertainty of its own. Lecture 9 introduces the t distribution that prices in this extra uncertainty, builds the confidence interval from it, and runs the course’s first formal test of a benchmark claim.

title: Lecture 8: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 55 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

What varies in a sampling distribution?
Why is \(E[\bar X]=\mu\) called unbiasedness?
What is the difference between an SD and an SE?
To cut an SE in half, by what factor must the sample size grow, and why?
What does the CLT say becomes approximately normal?
Why does a larger sample not remove selection bias?







Check your answers






The statistic varies across possible repeated samples; the parameter and the population stay fixed.
Its long-run average across repeated samples equals the population parameter.
An SD describes variation among observations; an SE describes variation of an estimator across samples.
By a factor of 4: the SE is proportional to \(1/\sqrt n\), so halving it requires \(2^2=4\) times the observations.
The standardised sample mean — and therefore, approximately, the sampling distribution of the mean. Not the original observations.
Sample size shrinks random error only. It does not change how units entered the sampling frame or the sample.






From worked to faded (5 minutes)
Re-read the worked SE calculation (Example 10.1). Then complete the same calculation for a proportion: a planned survey expects \(p=0.30\) and \(n=100\).
Step 1 (given). The SE formula for a proportion is \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\).
Step 2 (you). Calculate the SE.
Step 3 (you). Check the success–failure condition.






Check your answer





\(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{0.30(0.70)/100}\approx 0.0458\), about 4.6 percentage points. The expected counts are \(np=30\) successes and \(n(1-p)=70\) failures, both at least 10, so the normal approximation is acceptable.





Practice (10 minutes)

If \(\sigma=15\) and \(n=25\), find \(E[\bar X]\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\), and \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)\), naming the rule used at each step.
How large must \(n\) become to reduce an SE from 6 to 1.5?
For a sample proportion with \(\hat p\) expected near 0.50 and \(n=64\), calculate the SE and check the success–failure condition.
Explain why the normal approximation is more convincing in the right-hand panel of Figure 10.1.
State one threat to the CLT-based approximation that a large \(n\) alone does not solve.







Check your answers






\(E[\bar X]=\mu\) (linearity of expectation); \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n=225/25=9\) (variance of a scaled sum of independent variables); \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\sqrt 9=3\).
The SE must fall by a factor of 4, so the sample size must grow by \(4^2=16\) times.
\(\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/64}=0.0625\). Expected counts are 32 and 32, both at least 10.
Averaging 40 observations cancels more of the skewness and shrinks the sampling variation more than averaging 5 observations; the histogram hugs its normal curve far more closely.
Dependence between observations, or a non-representative sampling process. (Extreme outliers slow the approximation too.)






Widget homework (10 minutes)
Open the sampling-distribution lab again and run these three settings. For each, redraw several times and write one sentence on what the histogram of sample means shows:

\(n = 2\);
\(n = 25\);
\(n = 100\).







Check a model answer






At \(n=2\) the sample means scatter widely and their histogram is still right-skewed, echoing the population shape.
At \(n=25\) the histogram of means is clearly narrower and roughly symmetric, centred near 13.2.
At \(n=100\) the means form a tight bell around the population mean, with a typical deviation of less than one percentage point — the SE of about 0.84 made visible.






Spaced review: one item each from Lectures 7 and 6 (10 minutes)

(Lecture 7.) The sample variance divides by \(n-1\), not \(n\). In one or two sentences, why?
(Lecture 6.) Daily revenue is modelled as \(X\sim N(10, 2^2)\) (in thousands of euros). Find \(P(X>13)\).







Check your answers






The deviations are measured from the sample mean, which was itself estimated from the data; once it is fixed, only \(n-1\) deviations can vary freely, and dividing by \(n-1\) removes the resulting downward bias.
Standardise: \(z=(13-10)/2=1.5\), so \(P(X>13)=P(Z>1.5)\approx 0.067\).






Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question. Mean equity offered in the recorded-pitch frame is \(\mu=13.21\) with \(\sigma=8.44\). A random sample of \(n=100\) pitches is drawn. Using the CLT, find the probability that the sample mean exceeds 14.5 percentage points.






Check a model answer





By the CLT, \(\bar X\ \dot\sim\ N(13.21, 0.844^2)\) since \(\operatorname{SE}=8.44/\sqrt{100}=0.844\). Standardise: \(z=(14.5-13.21)/0.844\approx 1.53\), so \(P(\bar X>14.5)\approx P(Z>1.53)\approx 0.063\). About a 6% chance — and note the question is about the mean, not a single pitch: for one pitch the normal model was already rejected in Lecture 6.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture — or any business you know well. Name one number you would estimate from a sample (customer satisfaction, conversion rate, average basket size) and write two sentences: first say how you would draw the sample and roughly what SE-driven wobble you would tolerate, then say whether collecting four times the data would be worth halving that wobble for the decision at hand.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “I would estimate the conversion rate of tasting-stand visitors from a random 100 of them, and a wobble of about \(\pm 5\) percentage points is fine for deciding on a second stand. Collecting four times the data would halve that to about \(\pm 2.5\) points, which is not worth four more tasting days for this decision.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to help you sketch the sample-size trade-off for your own numbers.

Continue to Lecture 9: The t distribution, confidence intervals, and the two-sided test.
Formula sheet: Lecture 8 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 13 and 14.

text:
Before class
Tutorials are exam preparation sessions: every task below follows the format of the final exam. The standing routine for each task is the same — the TA states the task, pairs work on it first for a few minutes with AI use allowed, and the solution is then discussed in plenary, starting from the pair attempts.
This tutorial covers Lectures 6–8. The t distribution belongs to Lecture 9 and is rehearsed in Tutorial 4; everything here runs on the normal model and the CLT.
Bring your after-class work from Lectures 6–8. If the algebra is slowing you down, review Mathematics Refresher: sums, fractions, and roots.
Use the cumulative formula sheet through Lecture 8.
