title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors
text:
Standardising an observation \(x\) from \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) means calculating …
A parameter describes …
An estimator is …
The standard error of \(\bar X\) is …
The CLT describes …







Check your preparation






\(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\): the number of population SDs between \(x\) and the mean.
A parameter describes a population.
An estimator is a sample-based random rule used to estimate a parameter.
\(\sigma/\sqrt n\), estimated by \(S/\sqrt n\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown.
The approximate distribution of a properly standardised sum or mean: nearly normal for a large independent sample.
crumbs: 11  Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors
text:
In class
Attempt each task before opening its answer. A complete written answer names the quantity, shows the calculation, reports the value and units, interprets it in context, and states an important model or measurement boundary.

Task 1 — Population, frame, and claim
A student randomly selects 100 rows from the teaching file and estimates the mean initial equity offered.

State the population to which this design directly supports inference.
Explain why it does not represent all Shark Tank applicants.
Explain why it does not represent all US entrepreneurs.
State one change needed to target all US entrepreneurs.







Check your answer





The direct finite population is the 1,441 recorded pitches in completed Seasons 1–16. Applicants who were not televised are absent, so the frame does not represent all applicants. The show also selects a specialised group of entrepreneurs, not a probability sample of US entrepreneurs. Targeting all US entrepreneurs would require an appropriate national sampling frame and random selection from that frame.





Task 2 — Reproduce the realised sample
The sample is drawn with a visible seed, exactly as in Lecture 7, so every reader gets the same 100 rows:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

c(
  n = nrow(pitch_sample),
  mean_equity = mean(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sd_equity = sd(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  q1_equity = unname(quantile(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, 0.25)),
  median_equity = median(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  q3_equity = unname(quantile(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, 0.75)),
  deal_proportion = mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)
)

              n     mean_equity       sd_equity       q1_equity   median_equity 
     100.000000       12.760000        7.707887        8.000000       10.000000 
      q3_equity deal_proportion 
      17.750000        0.640000 



Identify the parameter, estimator, and estimate for mean equity.
Identify the parameter, estimator, and estimate for the deal proportion.
Calculate the IQR of equity and interpret it.
Explain why a different seed can produce different estimates and a different IQR.







Check your answer





For equity, the parameter is the population mean \(\mu\), the estimator is \(\bar X\), and the estimate is \(\bar x=12.76\). For deal outcome, the parameter is the population proportion \(p\), the estimator is \(\widehat P\), and the estimate is \(\hat p=0.64\). The sample quartiles are \(Q_1=8\) and \(Q_3=17.75\), so \(\operatorname{IQR}=17.75-8=9.75\) percentage points: the middle half of the sampled initial equity offers lies from 8% to 17.75%. A different seed selects a different random set of rows, so all realised sample statistics, including the IQR, can change.





Task 3 — Standard errors and sample size
Use the sample output above.

Estimate \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)\).
Estimate \(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)\).
Check the success–failure condition for \(\widehat P\).
Predict how each SE changes if \(n\) increases from 100 to 400 while the estimated spread remains similar.
The sample SD in part 1 was calculated with sd(), which divides by \(n-1\). State that number here and explain it in one sentence.







Check your answer





\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar X)=7.7079/\sqrt{100}=0.7708.
\]
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat P)
=\sqrt{0.64(0.36)/100}=0.0480.
\]
The sample contains 64 successes and 36 failures, so both are at least 10. Increasing \(n\) fourfold divides both SEs by \(\sqrt 4=2\). The divisor is \(n-1=99\): the deviations are measured from the estimated sample mean and must sum to zero, so only 99 of them vary freely, and dividing by 99 removes the resulting downward bias (Lecture 7).





Task 4 — One pitch versus one mean
Suppose the population mean is \(\mu=13.21\), the population SD is \(\sigma=8.44\), and samples of \(n=100\) are drawn independently.

State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar X\).
Calculate \(P(\bar X>15)\).
A classmate instead models a single pitch as \(X\sim N(13.21, 8.44^2)\) and calculates \(P(X>15)\). Compute that value too, and explain why the two answers are so different.
Which of the two normal models did Lecture 6 reject for equity offers, and why does the CLT nevertheless justify the calculation in part 2?







Check your answer





The CLT gives approximately \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(13.21,\,8.44^2/100)\), with SE \(0.844\). Therefore
\[
P(\bar X>15)
=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{15-13.21}{0.844}\right)
=1-\Phi(2.12)
\approx0.017.
\]
For a single pitch, \(z=(15-13.21)/8.44\approx0.21\), so \(P(X>15)\approx0.42\). The mean of 100 pitches varies ten times less than one pitch (\(\sigma/\sqrt{100}\)), so 15 is an ordinary value for one pitch but an extreme value for a mean of 100. Lecture 6 rejected the normal model for the pitch-level variable — equity offers are strongly right-skewed — so part 3 is a bad model. The CLT concerns the sample mean: averaging 100 independent draws produces a nearly normal sampling distribution even from a skewed population, which is why part 2 is defensible.





Task 5 — A proportion through the CLT
The frame deal proportion is \(p=0.612\). A random sample of \(n=100\) pitches is planned, with sample deal proportion \(\widehat P\).

Calculate \(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)\) and check the success–failure condition.
State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\widehat P\).
Approximate the probability that the sample shows a deal rate of at most 50%, i.e. \(P(\widehat P\le0.50)\).
Interpret the result in one sentence.







Check your answer





\(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{0.612(0.388)/100}\approx0.0487\); the expected counts are \(np=61.2\) and \(n(1-p)=38.8\), both at least 10. Hence \(\widehat P\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(0.612,\,0.0487^2)\). Standardise:
\[
z=\frac{0.50-0.612}{0.0487}\approx-2.30,
\qquad
P(\widehat P\le0.50)\approx\Phi(-2.30)\approx0.011.
\]
If the frame deal proportion is 61.2%, only about 1% of random samples of 100 would show a deal rate at or below 50% — such a sample would be surprising, the seed of the testing logic that Lecture 9 formalises.

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors
text:
After class

Timed individual practice — 12 minutes
Redo this unassisted and against the clock: no notes, no AI, formula sheet only — exam conditions. A random sample of 64 customers has mean monthly spending €82 and sample SD €24. Among the 64 customers, 40 renewed their subscription.

Estimate the SE of mean spending.
Estimate the SE of the renewal proportion and check its condition.
State what would happen to both SEs at \(n=256\).
Write one sentence distinguishing sampling uncertainty from selection bias.
Treating \(\mu=82\) and \(\sigma=24\) as the population values, use the CLT to approximate the probability that a new sample of 64 shows a mean above €85.







Check a model answer





The estimated SE of the mean is \(24/\sqrt{64}=3\) euros. The renewal estimate is \(40/64=0.625\), with estimated SE \(\sqrt{0.625(0.375)/64}\approx0.0605\); the sample has 40 successes and 24 failures, so the success–failure condition holds. Increasing the sample size from 64 to 256 would halve both SEs if the spread remained similar. These SEs describe random sample-to-sample variation, not bias created by an unrepresentative sampling frame. For the new sample, \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(82,3^2)\), so \(z=(85-82)/3=1\) and \(P(\bar X>85)\approx1-\Phi(1)\approx0.16\).





Check your understanding
Complete from memory:

A sampling distribution describes …
The standard error of a mean equals …
The success–failure condition requires …
The CLT says … becomes approximately normal.
A larger sample does not fix …







Check your answers






How a statistic would vary across repeated random samples.
\(\sigma/\sqrt n\) (estimated by \(S/\sqrt n\)).
\(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10\).
The standardised sample mean (and so, approximately, the sampling distribution of the mean) — not the original observations.
Selection bias: how units entered the frame or the sample.






Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture — or any business you know well. Pick one rate or average you could estimate from about 100 observations (conversion rate, average basket, renewal share), and write two sentences: first state the SE you would roughly expect and what range of sample outcomes would therefore be unsurprising, then say what observed value would genuinely surprise you — the instinct that next week’s hypothesis tests make exact.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “From 100 orders, a renewal share near 60% has an SE of about 5 points, so observed shares between roughly 50% and 70% would not surprise me. A share of 45% would — that is more than two SEs below what I believe, and that instinct is exactly what next week’s tests make precise.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this tutorial — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to sanity-check your SE guess for your own numbers.

Continue to Lecture 9: The t distribution, confidence intervals, and the two-sided test.

text:
Video preparation (20 minutes) Watch Confidence Intervals, Confidence Intervals When the Variance Is Unknown, and Introduction to Hypothesis Testing. Focus on repeated-sampling coverage, the t reference distribution, and the role of the null value. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.










Check your preparation





Let \(\delta=E[D]=\mu_X-15\). Then
\[
H_0:\delta=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\delta\ne0.
\]
This is equivalent to testing \(H_0:\mu_X=15\) against \(H_1:\mu_X\ne15\). Writing the contrast as \(\delta\) makes the central question “is the difference zero?” — the same structure later used for regression coefficients.

title: Lecture 9: The t distribution, confidence intervals, and the two-sided test
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Lecture 8 left us with a sample mean and its standard error. This lecture turns those two numbers into a defensible claim: a range of plausible values for the parameter, and a yes-or-no decision about a benchmark.

Video explanations (review): 20.5 Confidence Intervals, 20.7 Confidence Intervals with Unknown Variance, and Introduction to Hypothesis Testing.


From a benchmark to a zero contrast
The driving question compares a population mean to the benchmark 15. The prep exercise already made the key move: subtract the benchmark and study the gap
\[
D = X - 15,
\qquad
\delta = E[D] = \mu_X - 15.
\]
“Is mean equity different from 15?” becomes “is \(\delta\) different from zero?” This looks like a cosmetic rewrite, but it is the single most reusable idea of the next four weeks: every benchmark question can be turned into a question about a parameter being zero. Lecture 10 shows that group differences, proportion gaps, and regression slopes all wear the same zero-contrast uniform. Learn the pattern once here, and every later test is a rerun.


The price of estimating σ: the t distribution
Lecture 8 gave the standardised sample mean
\[
Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n},
\]
which is approximately standard normal by the CLT. But this \(Z\) contains the population SD \(\sigma\) — a number nobody knows in a real study. In practice we substitute the sample SD \(S\), and \(S\) is itself a random quantity: it changes from sample to sample, and in a small sample it can miss \(\sigma\) badly. Standardising with an estimated spread therefore produces a statistic that is more variable than \(Z\). For independent observations from a normal population,
\[
T=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}
\sim t_{n-1}.
\]
The t distribution is symmetric around zero like the standard normal, but it has heavier tails: extreme standardised values are more likely, precisely because \(S\) sometimes underestimates the true spread. Its degrees of freedom control how much heavier:

few degrees of freedom mean \(S\) is estimated imprecisely, so the tails are heavier;
more degrees of freedom mean more information about spread;
as the degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution approaches \(N(0,1)\).

For a one-sample mean, \(df=n-1\) — the same \(n-1\) you met in Lecture 7: once the sample mean is estimated, the \(n\) deviations must sum to zero, so only \(n-1\) of them vary freely when spread is estimated.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

t_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800)
curve_levels <- c("t, df = 4", "t, df = 10", "standard normal")
reference_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = t_grid, density = dt(t_grid, df = 4),
             curve = curve_levels[1]),
  data.frame(x = t_grid, density = dt(t_grid, df = 10),
             curve = curve_levels[2]),
  data.frame(x = t_grid, density = dnorm(t_grid),
             curve = curve_levels[3])
)
reference_curves$curve <- factor(reference_curves$curve,
                                 levels = curve_levels)
curve_colours <- c("t, df = 4" = "#D55E00",
                   "t, df = 10" = "#0072B2",
                   "standard normal" = "#009E73")

ggplot(reference_curves, aes(x, density,
                             colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.375, label = "t, df = 4",
           colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.335, label = "t, df = 10",
           colour = "#0072B2", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.295, label = "standard normal",
           colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = curve_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted"),
                        guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.41),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Standardised value", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 12.1: The t distribution for 4 and 10 degrees of freedom against the standard normal. All three are symmetric around zero; the t curves put more probability in the tails, most visibly at low degrees of freedom.





The difference in Figure 12.1 is most visible in the tails. This is why a 95% t critical value is larger than the normal 1.96 when \(df\) is small — the reference curve must reach further out to enclose 95% of its probability.
This resolves the prep prediction: replacing \(\sigma\) with \(S\) makes the interval wider, because the heavier-tailed t distribution demands a larger critical value. The extra width is the honest price of estimating one more quantity from the same data.






Check: which is larger, \(t_{0.975,11}\) or \(t_{0.975,99}\)?





\(t_{0.975,11}\approx 2.20\) is larger than \(t_{0.975,99}\approx 1.98\). With only 11 degrees of freedom, \(S\) is an imprecise estimate of \(\sigma\), so the t distribution has heavier tails and its 97.5% quantile sits further from zero. At \(df=99\) the critical value is already close to the normal 1.96 — with a large sample, the t and normal answers nearly coincide. Verify in R: qt(0.975, df = 11) and qt(0.975, df = 99).





The interval recipe
A confidence interval combines the estimate with its uncertainty. The general form is
\[
\text{estimate}
\ \pm\
\text{critical value}\times\text{standard error}.
\]
The product after the \(\pm\) is the margin of error. A confidence interval becomes:

wider when the confidence level increases (a larger critical value);
wider when observations are more variable (a larger SE);
narrower when the sample size increases, all else equal.

For an independent sample with unknown population SD,
\[
\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}
\]
is a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\). For a large independent sample, the interval is also a reasonable approximation when the population is not normal — the CLT again. The same recipe applied to the gap variable \(D\) gives an interval for \(\delta\).

Example 12.1 (Worked example: a 95% interval by hand) A random sample of \(n=64\) ventures reports a mean score of \(\bar x = 80\) with sample SD \(s = 16\). The industry benchmark is 75. Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\delta=\mu-75\), voicing every arithmetic step.

Estimate. The estimated gap is the sample mean minus the benchmark: \(\widehat\delta = 80 - 75 = 5\).
Standard error. \(\operatorname{SE}=s/\sqrt n = 16/\sqrt{64}\). The square root of 64 is 8, so \(\operatorname{SE}=16/8=2\).
Degrees of freedom and critical value. \(df=n-1=63\), and \(t_{0.975,63}\approx 2.00\) (the exam supplies this value; in R it is qt(0.975, df = 63), about 1.998).
Margin of error. Critical value times SE: \(2.00\times 2 = 4\).
Interval. Estimate plus and minus the margin: \(5 - 4 = 1\) and \(5 + 4 = 9\), so the 95% interval for \(\delta\) is \((1,\,9)\).

Every plausible value of the gap is positive: the data are consistent with a population mean between 1 and 9 points above the benchmark. Adding 75 back to both endpoints gives the equivalent interval \((76,\,84)\) for \(\mu\) itself — the gap form and the mean form are the same statement.



Check conditions before calculating
The formula is justified by the sampling design and distributional conditions, not by the presence of an R command. Before any interval or test, walk this checklist:

Random selection. Were the rows selected randomly from a defined frame? (Ours will be: the seed-123 sample of 100 from the 1,441-record frame.)
The 10% condition. Sampling without replacement creates weak dependence, but \(100/1441\approx 0.07 < 0.10\), so the usual independent-sample SE is a reasonable approximation.
Shape and sample size. Pitch-level equity is right-skewed, but \(n=100\) makes the t approximation for the sample mean far more credible than it would be for a very small sample. Still check for data errors or observations that dominate the mean.

These conditions support inference to the recorded-pitch frame. They do not make televised pitches representative of all entrepreneurs — the caveat box returns to this.


The Shark Tank case, with nothing hidden
Now the real question. The recipe runs on the reproducible sample of 100 from Lecture 7, and every object is constructed on screen:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

benchmark <- 15
pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp <-
  pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct - benchmark

gap_bar <- mean(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp)   # estimated gap
gap_sd  <- sd(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp)     # sample SD of the gap
n       <- nrow(pitch_sample)
df      <- n - 1
gap_se  <- gap_sd / sqrt(n)                   # standard error

c(
  sample_mean_equity = mean(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sample_mean_gap = gap_bar,
  sample_sd_gap = gap_sd,
  standard_error_gap = gap_se,
  degrees_of_freedom = df
)

sample_mean_equity    sample_mean_gap      sample_sd_gap standard_error_gap 
        12.7600000         -2.2400000          7.7078866          0.7707887 
degrees_of_freedom 
        99.0000000 


The estimated population mean gap is \(-2.24\) percentage points: the sample mean equity offer of 12.76 sits 2.24 points below the 15-point benchmark. Note that subtracting the constant 15 changes the mean but not the spread: gap_sd equals the sample SD of equity itself, 7.71.

critical_t <- qt(0.975, df = df)
gap_ci <- gap_bar + c(-1, 1) * critical_t * gap_se
mean_ci <- benchmark + gap_ci

c(critical_t = critical_t)

critical_t 
  1.984217 

c(gap_lower = gap_ci[1], gap_upper = gap_ci[2])

 gap_lower  gap_upper 
-3.7694119 -0.7105881 

c(mean_lower = mean_ci[1], mean_upper = mean_ci[2])

mean_lower mean_upper 
  11.23059   14.28941 


The 95% interval for the mean gap is approximately \((-3.77,\,-0.71)\) percentage points. Adding 15 to both endpoints gives the equivalent interval \((11.23,\,14.29)\) for mean initial equity. Same recipe as the hand-worked example — only the numbers changed.


A hypothesis test starts with a null model
The interval displays every plausible value. A test answers one question about one value. For a two-sided test,
\[
H_0:\delta=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\delta\ne0.
\]
The null says there is no population mean difference from the benchmark. The alternative allows a difference in either direction. Choose the two-sided alternative from the research question before inspecting the sample estimate. (Directional, one-sided alternatives exist; Lecture 10 treats them and explains when they are — and are not — legitimate.)
Standardise the estimated gap using its SE:
\[
T=
\frac{\widehat\delta-0}
{\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\delta)}
=
\frac{\bar D}{S_D/\sqrt n}.
\]
By hand first, from the numbers already on screen: the estimate is \(-2.24\), its SE is \(0.77\), so
\[
t=\frac{-2.24}{0.77}\approx -2.91.
\]
The sign records direction — below the benchmark; the absolute value records distance from zero in standard-error units — almost three SEs. Now the same calculation in R, with the p-value:

t_value <- gap_bar / gap_se
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df)

c(
  estimate = gap_bar,
  standard_error = gap_se,
  t_statistic = t_value,
  degrees_of_freedom = df,
  two_sided_p_value = p_value
)

          estimate     standard_error        t_statistic degrees_of_freedom 
      -2.240000000        0.770788656       -2.906114385       99.000000000 
 two_sided_p_value 
       0.004515396 




A two-sided p-value uses both tails
The p-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\), of obtaining a test statistic at least as far from zero as the observed statistic in either direction:
\[
p=P\!\left(|T_{99}|\ge|t_{obs}|\mid H_0\right).
\]


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]
pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp <- pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct - 15
gap_bar <- mean(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp)
gap_se <- sd(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp) / sqrt(nrow(pitch_sample))
df <- nrow(pitch_sample) - 1
t_value <- gap_bar / gap_se

null_curve <- data.frame(x = seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 1200))
null_curve$density <- dt(null_curve$x, df = df)
left_tail <- subset(null_curve, x <= -abs(t_value))
right_tail <- subset(null_curve, x >= abs(t_value))

ggplot(null_curve, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(data = left_tail, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_area(data = right_tail, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(t_value), abs(t_value)),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = -abs(t_value), y = 0.33,
           label = "t == -2.91", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = 1.15) +
  annotate("text", x = abs(t_value), y = 0.33,
           label = "t == +2.91", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = -0.15) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "t statistic under the null", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 12.2: The t distribution with 99 degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis. Dashed lines mark statistics as far from zero as the observed t = −2.91; the two orange tail areas together are the two-sided p-value, about 0.005.





Read Figure 12.2 with the five-step sequence. (1) The curve is the distribution of the t statistic if the null were true — not data, a null model. (2) The horizontal axis is the possible t statistic; the vertical axis is density, so probability is area. (3) The dashed lines mark \(-2.91\) and \(+2.91\): statistics as far from zero as the one observed. (4) The pattern: the two orange tail areas beyond the dashed lines are tiny — together about 0.0045. (5) Takeaway: if the true mean gap were zero, a sample as extreme as ours would occur in roughly 5 of every 1,000 samples. That is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and not the size of the gap.
At \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\) because \(p<0.05\). The random sample provides evidence that mean initial equity in the recorded-pitch frame differs from 15 percentage points; the negative estimate indicates that it is lower.


The confidence interval and test tell the same story
For the same two-sided t procedure:

reject \(H_0:\delta=0\) at level \(\alpha\) exactly when the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval excludes zero;
do not reject when the interval includes zero.

Here the gap interval \((-3.77,\,-0.71)\) excludes zero, matching the rejection. The interval adds information the p-value does not: it displays the direction, plausible magnitude, and precision of the difference. Course policy, from here to the end of Intermediate: report the estimate and interval alongside any test decision.






Try it: read the decision straight from an interval





A colleague reports a 95% confidence interval for a mean gap: \((-1.4,\,3.8)\) percentage points. No t statistic, no p-value.
Step 1 (given). The matched two-sided test rejects \(H_0:\delta=0\) at 5% exactly when the 95% interval excludes zero.
Step 2 (you). Does this interval exclude zero? State the test decision without computing anything.
Step 3 (you). What may you conclude about the population mean gap — and what may you not conclude?






Check your answer





Zero lies inside \((-1.4,\,3.8)\), so the 5% two-sided test does not reject \(H_0:\delta=0\). The data are compatible with a zero gap — and also with gaps as large as 3.8 points in one direction and 1.4 in the other. You may not conclude that the gap is zero: “do not reject” is not “accept,” a distinction Lecture 10 builds on.








Interpret 95% confidence correctly
The parameter is fixed; interval endpoints vary from sample to sample. “95%” describes the procedure: if the same valid recipe were repeated on many random samples, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the parameter.
The simulation in Figure 12.3 repeats the random sample and interval calculation 100 times. The fixed target is the mean initial equity among all 1,441 recorded pitches.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(209)
B_coverage <- 100
n_coverage <- 100
target_mean <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
ci_lower <- ci_upper <- ci_centre <- numeric(B_coverage)

for (i in seq_len(B_coverage)) {
  repeated_sample <- sample(
    sharks$equity_offered_pct,
    size = n_coverage,
    replace = FALSE
  )
  repeated_mean <- mean(repeated_sample)
  repeated_se <- sd(repeated_sample) / sqrt(n_coverage)
  repeated_critical <- qt(0.975, df = n_coverage - 1)
  ci_centre[i] <- repeated_mean
  ci_lower[i] <- repeated_mean - repeated_critical * repeated_se
  ci_upper[i] <- repeated_mean + repeated_critical * repeated_se
}

intervals <- data.frame(
  lower = ci_lower, centre = ci_centre, upper = ci_upper,
  covers = ifelse(ci_lower <= target_mean & ci_upper >= target_mean,
                  "contains the target mean", "misses the target mean")
)
intervals <- intervals[order(intervals$centre), ]
intervals$position <- seq_len(B_coverage)

ggplot(intervals, aes(y = position, colour = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = position),
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(x = centre), size = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = target_mean, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#C98B2E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = target_mean, y = B_coverage + 3.5,
           label = "mu == 13.21", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("contains the target mean" = "#009E73",
                                 "misses the target mean" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Mean initial equity offered (%)",
       y = "Repeated sample (ordered by estimate)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )








Figure 12.3: One hundred repetitions of the same procedure: draw 100 random pitches, compute a 95% t interval for mean initial equity. Green intervals contain the fixed target mean (gold dashed line); orange intervals miss it. In this run, 96 of 100 intervals cover the target.





Each horizontal segment in Figure 12.3 is one 95% confidence interval; its dot is that sample’s mean. The gold dashed vertical line is the fixed target mean, 13.21. In this run (seed 209), 96 of 100 intervals cross the line. A new run need not give exactly 95, but across many repetitions the proportion approaches 95% when the procedure’s conditions hold.
One sentence is now forbidden for the rest of your studies:

“There is a 95% probability that the population mean is in my interval.”

The realised interval \((11.23, 14.29)\) either contains the fixed parameter or it does not — there is no probability left once the sample is drawn. The correct replacement:

“This interval was produced by a procedure that captures the fixed population mean in about 95% of repeated valid samples.”


What significance can and cannot tell you
Three boundaries around everything in this lecture. First, significance is not importance: \(p\approx 0.005\) says the gap is measured precisely enough to distinguish it from zero, not that a 2.24-point gap matters for any decision — magnitude and context decide that. Second, significance is not causation: the evidence concerns a mean in an observational frame; nothing here says why equity asks sit below 15 points. Third, a narrow interval repairs nothing about selection: the interval quantifies random sampling error within the recorded-pitch frame. If the frame itself is a producer-curated selection of telegenic pitches — and it is — then no interval width, however impressive, extends the conclusion to entrepreneurs in general. An on-air agreement is still not a completed investment.



Answering the driving question
Yes — within the frame. The seed-123 sample gives an estimated gap of \(-2.24\) percentage points with SE \(0.77\); the 95% interval for mean equity is \((11.23, 14.29)\), which excludes 15, and the two-sided test rejects \(H_0:\delta=0\) at 5% (\(t=-2.91\), \(p\approx 0.005\)). The evidence says the frame’s mean initial equity ask sits below 15 percent — plausibly by between 0.7 and 3.8 points. Whether that gap matters commercially, and what caused it, are separate questions the test cannot answer.
Next: We can now test a benchmark and report the answer as an interval and a p-value. But every test decision can be wrong in one of two ways — rejecting a true null, or missing a real effect — and the two mistakes rarely cost the same. Lecture 10 names the two error types, shows the four levers that make wrong calls rarer (power), settles when a one-sided alternative is legitimate, and then opens the door this whole course has been walking toward: the same estimate–SE–t–p–interval row, sitting in a regression table.

title: Lecture 9: The t distribution, confidence intervals, and the two-sided test
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 60 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

Why does replacing \(\sigma\) with the sample SD \(S\) require a t rather than a normal reference distribution?
Why does a one-sample t procedure use \(n-1\) degrees of freedom?
What are the three pieces of a confidence interval?
What do \(H_0:\delta=0\) and \(H_1:\delta\ne0\) say?
Why does a two-sided p-value use two tails?
What is the exact decision link between a 95% t interval and a 5% two-sided t-test?







Check your answers






\(S\) is itself estimated and varies from sample to sample; the t distribution’s heavier tails represent that extra uncertainty.
Estimating the sample mean imposes one constraint (deviations sum to zero) before spread is estimated, leaving \(n-1\) freely varying deviations.
Estimate, critical value, and standard error.
The null states that the population contrast is zero; the alternative allows a non-zero contrast in either direction.
Values equally far below and above zero are both evidence against a two-sided null.
The test rejects exactly when the interval excludes zero, provided both use the same model and SE.






From worked to faded (10 minutes)
Re-read the hand-worked interval (Example 12.1). Then complete the same calculation with new numbers: \(n=25\) customers, mean satisfaction \(\bar x = 42\), sample SD \(s = 10\), benchmark 40, so \(\delta=\mu-40\).
Step 1 (given). The estimated gap is \(42-40=2\), and \(t_{0.975,24}\approx 2.06\).
Step 2 (you). Calculate the SE and the margin of error.
Step 3 (you). Write the 95% interval for \(\delta\) and state, without any further computation, the 5% two-sided test decision.






Check your answer





\(\operatorname{SE}=10/\sqrt{25}=2\); margin of error \(2.06\times 2=4.13\). The interval is \(2\pm 4.13=(-2.13,\,6.13)\). Zero lies inside, so the 5% two-sided test does not reject \(H_0:\delta=0\): the data are compatible with a zero gap — and with gaps up to about 6 points. (For completeness, \(t=2/2=1.00\), \(p\approx 0.33\).)





Practice (10 minutes)

A sample has \(n=49\), \(\bar x=110\), and \(s=14\). Define \(\delta=\mu-100\). Construct a 95% interval for \(\delta\) (use \(t_{0.975,48}\approx 2.01\)).
Test \(H_0:\delta=0\) against \(H_1:\delta\ne0\) at 5%. Report the statistic, degrees of freedom, approximate p-value, decision, and a contextual conclusion.
A coefficient-like estimate is 0.42 percentage points per €100,000, with SE 0.18 and \(df=120\). Test a two-sided zero null and construct a 95% interval (use \(t_{0.975,120}\approx 1.98\)).
Explain why a statistically significant mean gap need not be practically important or causal.







Check your answers






The estimated gap is \(110-100=10\), its SE is \(14/\sqrt{49}=2\), and the interval is \(10\pm 2.01(2)=(5.98,\,14.02)\).
\(t=10/2=5.00\), \(df=48\), two-sided p-value below 0.001. Reject \(H_0\): the data provide strong evidence that the population mean exceeds 100 — plausibly by 6 to 14 points.
\(t=0.42/0.18\approx 2.33\), two-sided p-value about 0.021. The 95% interval is \(0.42\pm1.98(0.18)=(0.064,\,0.776)\) percentage points per €100,000. Reject the zero null at 5%.
Statistical significance concerns precision relative to zero. Practical importance depends on the magnitude and the decision context, and causality requires an appropriate design and assumptions — neither is delivered by a small p-value.






Rewrite the forbidden sentence (5 minutes)
Rewrite this claim correctly: “There is a 95% chance that the population mean is in my interval \((11.23, 14.29)\).”






Check a model answer





“The interval \((11.23, 14.29)\) was produced by a procedure that captures the fixed population mean in about 95% of repeated valid samples.” The parameter is fixed; it is the interval endpoints that vary across samples, as in Figure 12.3.





Spaced review: one item each from Lectures 8 and 4 (10 minutes)

(Lecture 8.) A planned survey expects a sample SD around 24 with \(n=64\). Estimate the SE of the sample mean, and state what happens to it if \(n\) grows to 256.
(Lecture 4.) From the 2×2 counts table, \(P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688\) while \(P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 0.573\). Why are these two numbers different even though both involve the same 505 records?







Check your answers






\(\operatorname{SE}=24/\sqrt{64}=3\). Quadrupling the sample size halves the SE to 1.5 — the square-root rule.
They condition on different reference classes: the first divides the 505 joint records by the 734 late-season records, the second divides the same 505 by the 882 deal records. Changing the event after the bar changes the denominator.






Worked exam interpretation (10 minutes)
Question (Mock Exam Q4 pattern). From a frame of 1,000 accelerator applicants, a simple random sample of 64 was selected. prep_hours is hours spent preparing the application; \(\mu\) is the frame mean. The sample has \(\bar x=18.4\) and \(s=8.0\). R produced:
One Sample t-test

data: prep_hours
t = 2.400, df = 63, p-value = 0.0193
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 16
95 percent confidence interval:
 16.40 20.40
sample estimate:
mean of x = 18.40
Verify the SE and the t statistic, explain the degrees of freedom, interpret the p-value and the interval, and give the 5% decision.






Check a model answer





\(\operatorname{SE}=8/\sqrt{64}=1\) hour, so \(t=(18.4-16)/1=2.4\), matching the output. \(df=64-1=63\) because the deviations from the estimated sample mean must sum to zero, leaving 63 free. If the frame mean were 16 hours, a sample mean at least 2.4 SEs from 16 in either direction would occur in about 1.9% of random samples; since \(0.0193<0.05\), reject \(H_0:\mu=16\). The interval \((16.40, 20.40)\) gives the plausible range for \(\mu\) — it excludes 16, agreeing with the test — and was produced by a procedure with about 95% coverage across repeated samples. The claim concerns the 1,000-applicant frame, not applicants in general.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture — or any business you know well. Pick one key metric with a published industry benchmark (conversion rate, average order value, churn), frame the comparison as a gap \(\delta = \mu - \text{benchmark}\), and write two sentences: first say what sample you could realistically collect and what a 95% interval for \(\delta\) excluding zero would let you claim, then say what decision would change if the interval turned out to include zero.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “The sector churn benchmark is 25% per term; from my roughly 120 subscribers I can estimate \(\delta = \mu - 25\), and a 95% interval sitting entirely below zero would let me claim genuinely stickier customers in my pitch. If the interval included zero, I would stop pitching retention as my edge and lead with margin instead.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to check whether your gap is defined on a population you can actually sample.

Continue to Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression.
Formula sheet: Lecture 9 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 15 and 16.

title: Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Lecture 9 delivered one complete test. This final lecture makes testing a routine: one recipe, an honest account of the two ways any decision can be wrong, and the payoff — the same machinery reappearing, unchanged, in every regression table you will read from Intermediate onwards.

Video explanations (review): Introduction to Hypothesis Testing and Type I and Type II Errors.


Why zero is the universal benchmark
Many empirical questions ask whether a population contrast is absent:

difference from a target: \(\delta=\mu-15\);
difference in probabilities: \(\delta_p=p-0.50\);
difference between two group means: \(\mu_1-\mu_0\);
a regression slope: \(\beta_j\).

In every case, “no difference” or “no linear association” becomes
\[
H_0:\theta=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\theta\ne0.
\]
Testing a non-zero benchmark can always be rewritten as a test of a zero-valued contrast — Lecture 9’s gap device. This common structure is the bridge from Basic inference to regression inference: learn to test one zero, and you can test them all.


The seven-step testing workflow
Use the same sequence every time — on the exam, in your EiA venture, in any report you ever write:

Define the population parameter and its units.
State \(H_0\) and the two-sided \(H_1\) before inspecting the result.
Check the sampling and model conditions.
Calculate the estimate and its SE under the null model.
Standardise: \((\text{estimate}-0)/\text{SE}\).
Calculate the two-sided p-value and compare it with the pre-specified significance level \(\alpha\).
Report the estimate, uncertainty, decision, contextual meaning, and limits.

The significance level \(\alpha\) is a long-run decision threshold, commonly 0.05, fixed in advance. The p-value is calculated from the observed data under \(H_0\). They are not the same object: one is a rule, the other a result.
If \(p\le\alpha\), reject \(H_0\). If \(p>\alpha\), do not reject \(H_0\) — and do not say “accept \(H_0\).” This resolves the prep prediction: a study with \(p=0.20\) has not shown the null is true; it may simply lack the precision to distinguish a meaningful non-zero parameter from zero. The power section below makes that precise.

Example 13.1 (Worked example: a proportion test by hand) An accelerator claims that half of its alumni launch a trading venture within a year. In a random sample of 400 former participants, 232 had launched. Let \(p\) be the launch proportion in the alumni frame and define \(\delta_p=p-0.50\). Test \(H_0:\delta_p=0\) against \(H_1:\delta_p\ne0\) at 5%, voicing every arithmetic step.

Estimate. \(\hat p=232/400=0.58\), so the estimated gap is \(\widehat\delta_p=0.58-0.50=0.08\), eight percentage points.
Conditions under the null. \(np_0=400(0.50)=200\) and \(n(1-p_0)=200\), both far above 10 — the normal approximation is safe.
Null SE. Under \(H_0\) the true proportion is 0.50, so \(\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/400}=\sqrt{0.25/400}
=\sqrt{0.000625}=0.025\).
Standardise. \(z=0.08/0.025=3.20\): the observed gap sits 3.2 null standard errors above zero.
p-value and decision. The two-sided p-value is \(2\,P(Z\le-3.20)\approx 0.0014 < 0.05\): reject \(H_0\). The sample provides strong evidence that the frame launch proportion differs from 50%; the positive estimate places it above.

Note step 4’s subtlety: the SE was computed with \(p_0=0.50\), not with \(\hat p\) — the test measures how surprising the sample is in the null’s world, so the null supplies the spread.



The Shark Tank deal proportion, in R
The same recipe on our reproducible sample of 100: is the frame’s deal proportion different from 50%? Every object is constructed on screen:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

n <- nrow(pitch_sample)
phat <- mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)   # sample deal proportion
p0 <- 0.50                                # null value
deal_gap <- phat - p0                     # estimated gap

c(n = n, phat = phat, p0 = p0, deal_gap = deal_gap)

       n     phat       p0 deal_gap 
  100.00     0.64     0.50     0.14 



null_se <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
z_value <- deal_gap / null_se
two_sided_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_value))

c(
  null_standard_error = null_se,
  z_statistic = z_value,
  two_sided_p_value = two_sided_p
)

null_standard_error         z_statistic   two_sided_p_value 
        0.050000000         2.800000000         0.005110261 


The estimate is \(\widehat\delta_p=0.14\), fourteen percentage points. The null SE is \(\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/100}=0.05\), the statistic is \(z=2.80\), and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. The success–failure condition holds under the null: \(np_0=50\) and \(n(1-p_0)=50\). Reject the zero-gap null at 5%: the random sample provides evidence that the recorded-pitch-frame deal proportion differs from 50%, and the positive estimate places it above.


Interval and test: report both
Step 7 of the workflow says a decision alone is not a report. A large-sample 95% interval for the proportion uses the estimated SE:
\[
\hat p\pm1.96
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}.
\]

estimated_se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
proportion_ci <- phat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * estimated_se
gap_ci <- proportion_ci - p0

c(proportion_lower = proportion_ci[1],
  proportion_upper = proportion_ci[2])

proportion_lower proportion_upper 
         0.54592          0.73408 

c(gap_lower = gap_ci[1], gap_upper = gap_ci[2])

gap_lower gap_upper 
  0.04592   0.23408 


The proportion interval is approximately \((0.546,\,0.734)\); the equivalent gap interval is \((0.046,\,0.234)\), which excludes zero and agrees with the test decision here.

Optional: estimated versus null standard errors Look closely: the test divided by the null SE \(\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}=0.050\), while the interval used the estimated SE \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}=0.048\). The test asks how surprising the sample is if \(H_0\) were true, so the null supplies the spread; the interval makes no null assumption, so the data supply it. Because these are not exactly the same procedure, interval and test decisions need not match perfectly when a result sits very near the boundary. Exact equivalence requires an interval obtained by inverting the same test — beyond this course. For the mean-gap t procedures of Lecture 9 the same SE is used in both, so there the match is exact.



What a p-value is not
The two-sided p-value is
\[
P\!\left(|\text{test statistic}|
\ge|\text{observed statistic}|\mid H_0\right)
\]
— and nothing else. Before the break you receive four sentences about the launch test of Example 13.1 (\(z=3.20\), \(p\approx 0.0014\)). Each one is wrong. In pairs, correct all four; the plenary compares repairs.






Try it: correct the four wrong p-value sentences





Sentence 1 (you). “There is only a 0.14% probability that the launch proportion really is 50%.”
Sentence 2 (you). “The result has a 0.14% probability of being due to chance.”
Sentence 3 (you). “Such a tiny p-value shows that the launch proportion is far above 50%.”
Sentence 4 (you). “The tiny p-value proves that the accelerator causes its alumni to launch ventures.”






Check your answers






A p-value is not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\). Correct: “If the launch proportion were exactly 50%, a sample gap at least this far from zero in either direction would occur in about 0.14% of random samples.”
The p-value is computed assuming chance alone (the null model) generated the gap; it is the probability of data this extreme under that assumption, not the probability that the assumption holds.
A p-value measures surprise, not size. The magnitude is the estimate: 8 percentage points, with an interval around it. A tiny p-value can accompany a tiny gap when \(n\) is huge.
Significance says nothing about why. Alumni self-selected into the accelerator; without a design that isolates its effect, “causes” is unsupported. Correct: the frame’s launch proportion differs from 50%.









Type I error, Type II error, and power
A test is a decision rule, and any decision rule can be wrong in exactly two ways:



Reality
Reject \(H_0\)
Do not reject \(H_0\)




\(H_0\) true
Type I error
Correct decision


\(H_1\) true
Correct decision
Type II error



The significance level controls the first:
\[
P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true})=\alpha.
\]
Power is the ability to avoid the second:
\[
\text{power}=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_1\text{ true}).
\]
For the launch test, in context: a Type I error would be concluding that the alumni launch proportion differs from 50% when it is exactly 50% — crying wolf about a fictitious difference, embarrassing the analyst who advises repricing the programme. A Type II error would be failing to detect a launch proportion that genuinely differs from 50% — missing a real signal because the sample was too small or noisy.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

z_grid <- seq(-4.5, 6.5, length.out = 1600)
critical <- qnorm(0.975)
panel_levels <- c("Null is true", "An alternative value is true")

test_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(z = z_grid, density = dnorm(z_grid, mean = 0),
             panel = panel_levels[1]),
  data.frame(z = z_grid, density = dnorm(z_grid, mean = 2.5),
             panel = panel_levels[2])
)
test_curves$panel <- factor(test_curves$panel, levels = panel_levels)

rejection <- subset(test_curves, z <= -critical | z >= critical)
rejection$side <- ifelse(rejection$z < 0, "left", "right")

panel_labels <- data.frame(
  z = c(0, 3.6),
  density = c(0.13, 0.14),
  label = c("do not reject", "power"),
  panel = factor(panel_levels[c(1, 2)], levels = panel_levels)
)
alpha_labels <- data.frame(
  z = c(-2.5, 2.5),
  density = c(0.028, 0.028),
  label = c("alpha/2", "alpha/2"),
  panel = factor(panel_levels[c(1, 1)], levels = panel_levels)
)

ggplot(test_curves, aes(z, density)) +
  geom_area(data = rejection, aes(group = side, fill = panel),
            alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-critical, critical), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = panel), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = panel_labels, aes(label = label),
            colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(data = alpha_labels, aes(label = label), parse = TRUE,
            colour = "#17324D", size = 3.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "fixed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Null is true" = "#D55E00",
                               "An alternative value is true" = "#009E73"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Null is true" = "#17324D",
                                 "An alternative value is true" = "#0072B2"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 6)) +
  labs(x = "z statistic", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )








Figure 13.1: Two-sided testing at α = 0.05. Left: when the null is true, the z statistic follows the dark curve and the orange rejection regions have total probability 0.05 — the Type I error rate. Right: when a positive alternative is true, the statistic follows the shifted blue curve; the green area is the power, and the unshaded middle is the Type II error probability. Both panels use the same axes.





In both panels of Figure 13.1, the horizontal axis is the possible z statistic, the vertical axis is density, and probability is area. The dashed vertical lines mark the same two-sided critical values, \(\pm 1.96\). In the left panel the null is true: the two orange rejection tails have total probability \(\alpha=0.05\), which is exactly the Type I error rate — the test is built to cry wolf 5% of the time. In the right panel a particular positive alternative is true, so the curve has shifted: the green area is the power, and whatever probability remains between the dashed lines is the Type II error rate.
Four levers raise power:

a larger true distance from zero (an effect that is easier to see);
a larger sample (a smaller SE);
lower unexplained variation (also a smaller SE);
a larger \(\alpha\) — but this lever is a trade-off, not a free gain: widening the rejection region catches more true effects and raises the Type I error rate in lockstep.



One-sided alternatives
A two-sided test asks whether a parameter differs from zero in either direction. A one-sided test asks a directional question chosen before the sample is examined:



Research question
Alternative
Relevant tail(s)




Does the gap differ from zero?
\(H_1:\delta\ne0\)
both tails


Is the gap below zero?
\(H_1:\delta<0\)
left tail


Is the gap above zero?
\(H_1:\delta>0\)
right tail



In all three cases the test statistic is compared with its distribution under the zero boundary \(H_0:\delta=0\). What changes is which values count as evidence for the stated alternative — that is, where the rejection region sits.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

alpha_tail <- 0.05
tail_df <- 99
tail_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1400)
critical_two <- qt(c(alpha_tail / 2, 1 - alpha_tail / 2), df = tail_df)
critical_left <- qt(alpha_tail, df = tail_df)
critical_right <- qt(1 - alpha_tail, df = tail_df)

panel_levels <- c("Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided")
null_curve <- do.call(rbind, lapply(panel_levels, function(p) {
  data.frame(x = tail_grid, density = dt(tail_grid, df = tail_df),
             panel = p)
}))
null_curve$panel <- factor(null_curve$panel, levels = panel_levels)

rejection <- rbind(
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Two-sided" & x <= critical_two[1]),
        side = "left"),
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Two-sided" & x >= critical_two[2]),
        side = "right"),
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Left-sided" & x <= critical_left),
        side = "left"),
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Right-sided" & x >= critical_right),
        side = "right")
)

critical_lines <- data.frame(
  x = c(critical_two, critical_left, critical_right),
  panel = factor(c("Two-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided"),
                 levels = panel_levels)
)

panel_labels <- data.frame(
  x = c(-2.8, 2.8, -2.8, 2.8, 0, 0, 0),
  density = c(0.035, 0.035, 0.035, 0.035, 0.42, 0.42, 0.42),
  label = c("2.5%", "2.5%", "5%", "5%",
            "H[1] : delta != 0", "H[1] : delta < 0", "H[1] : delta > 0"),
  parse_me = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),
  panel = factor(c("Two-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided",
                   "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided"),
                 levels = panel_levels)
)

ggplot(null_curve, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(data = rejection, aes(group = side),
            fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(data = critical_lines, aes(xintercept = x),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = subset(panel_labels, !parse_me), aes(label = label),
            colour = "#17324D", size = 2.9) +
  geom_text(data = subset(panel_labels, parse_me), aes(label = label),
            parse = TRUE, colour = "#5B6976", size = 3.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = "fixed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-3, 0, 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4), limits = c(0, 0.44),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "t statistic", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )








Figure 13.2: Rejection regions at α = 0.05 for the two-sided and both one-sided alternatives, on the same null t distribution (df = 99). The two-sided test places 2.5% in each tail; a one-sided test moves the full 5% into the tail named by its alternative, so its critical value is closer to zero in that direction.





Compare Figure 13.2 with the left panel of Figure 13.1: same logic, different placement of the 5%. Moving the full 5% into one tail pulls that critical value closer to zero, so a one-sided test is more able to detect an effect in its chosen direction — a power gain. The price: results in the opposite direction, however extreme, do not support the stated alternative at all.
That power gain is exactly why the direction must follow from the research question and be fixed before the data are inspected. Choosing the tail because the observed estimate happens to point that way — or simply to obtain a smaller p-value — silently doubles the true Type I error rate: you would take the 5% tail on whichever side the noise landed. For Lecture 9’s equity-gap statistic, \(t=-2.91\) with \(df=99\):

the two-sided p-value is about 0.0045;
a pre-specified left-sided alternative \(H_1:\delta<0\) gives about 0.0023;
a pre-specified right-sided alternative \(H_1:\delta>0\) gives about 0.9977.

The negative estimate agrees with the left-sided alternative and points away from the right-sided one. Course convention, on the exam and in every chapter: tests are two-sided, because in business research a difference in either direction is usually relevant — and because the convention removes any temptation to pick the convenient tail.


Preview: the test attached to a regression slope
R applies the same zero-null logic to every regression coefficient. Consider the simple model of initial equity offered on season, fitted to all 1,441 records:

preview_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks)
summary(preview_model)$coefficients

              Estimate Std. Error   t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 20.4565874 0.46442667  44.04697 4.922706e-269
season      -0.8241241 0.04752298 -17.34159  2.514546e-61

confint(preview_model)

                 2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 19.5455616 21.3676132
season      -0.9173458 -0.7309023


Read the season row with the vocabulary you now own. The estimate is \(-0.824\): about 0.82 percentage points less equity offered per additional season. The SE, 0.048, is its sampling uncertainty in the same units. The t value, \(-17.3\), is estimate divided by SE — step 5 of the workflow. The p-value belongs to the printed two-sided test
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\beta_1\ne0,
\]
and the 95% interval \((-0.92,\,-0.73)\) excludes zero, agreeing with the rejection. Every column is a Lecture 9–10 object wearing a regression name. What the row does not say: this is an observational time association, not a causal effect of moving a pitch to a later season.
Intermediate begins from this familiar estimate–SE–t–p-value structure and adds careful coefficient interpretation, multiple predictors, and model diagnostics.

What a significant result does and does not establish
Three separations to carry out of this course. Significance is not magnitude: a tiny effect can be significant in a large sample, and a meaningful effect can be non-significant in a small or noisy one — the p-value measures surprise under the null, the estimate measures size. Significance is not causation: none of this lecture’s machinery knows whether the predictor was randomly assigned. And no test repairs the frame: selection into the recorded-pitch file, measurement of “deal” as an on-air agreement, and dependence between observations are untouched by any p-value. The standing reporting list, for every analysis from now on: the estimate in substantive units; a confidence interval; the p-value or decision; whether the magnitude matters for the business question; and the sampling, measurement, and causal limits.



Answering the driving question
The two wrong calls: rejecting a true null (Type I, rate set by \(\alpha\)) and missing a true effect (Type II, rate cut by power). Wrong calls become rarer with more data, less noise, bigger true effects — and, for Type I only, a stricter \(\alpha\), at the price of more Type II. And the regression table? Each coefficient row is a Lecture 9 test: estimate, SE, t, two-sided p against zero, interval.
That closes the arc of QM Basic. Ten lectures ago a Shark Tank pitch was an anecdote. Now you can define events and variables on a frame, describe their distributions, condition without confusing directions, model sampling variation, and turn “our sample mean is 12.76” into a defensible, properly hedged claim about a population — with its uncertainty, its decision, and its limits stated. That is the difference between an opinion with a spreadsheet and evidence.
Next: Tutorial 4 rehearses Lectures 9–10 in exam format, and the Mock Exam then integrates the whole course under exam conditions. The story itself continues next year: QM Intermediate picks up exactly where today’s regression preview left off, and the coefficient row you can already read becomes the central object of six lectures on linear regression.

title: Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 65 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

Why can most comparison hypotheses be written as a parameter equal to zero?
What is the difference between \(\alpha\) and a p-value?
What is a Type I error?
What is a Type II error?
Name three factors that increase power.
Why is “do not reject” different from “accept”?
What does \(H_0:\beta_j=0\) mean in a regression model?







Check your answers






Subtracting the benchmark or reference value creates a contrast; “no difference” corresponds to a zero contrast.
\(\alpha\) is a pre-specified long-run decision threshold; the p-value is calculated from the observed statistic under the null.
Rejecting \(H_0\) when it is true.
Not rejecting \(H_0\) when a specified alternative is true.
Any three of: larger sample size, larger true effect, lower noise, or larger \(\alpha\) (the last at the cost of more Type I errors).
A non-significant result may simply be too imprecise to distinguish a meaningful parameter from zero.
Holding the other included predictors fixed, the population-model coefficient for predictor \(j\) is zero.






From worked to faded, then unassisted (20 minutes)
Re-read the hand-worked launch test (Example 13.1). Then complete the same recipe with new numbers: in 200 independent trials there are 120 successes, and the benchmark is \(p_0=0.50\).
Step 1 (given). \(\hat p=120/200=0.60\), so \(\widehat\delta_p=0.10\); the null counts are \(200(0.50)=100\) successes and 100 failures, both above 10.
Step 2 (you). Calculate the null SE and the z statistic.
Step 3 (you). The two-sided p-value and the 5% decision, in context.






Check your answer





\(\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/200}\approx 0.0354\), so \(z=0.10/0.0354\approx 2.83\) and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. Reject the zero-gap null at 5%: the data provide evidence that the success proportion differs from 50%, with the positive estimate placing it above.



Now unassisted:

A sample of \(n=49\) difference scores has \(\bar d=3\) and \(s_d=14\). Test \(H_0:\delta=0\) against \(H_1:\delta\ne0\) at 5%.
Describe the Type I and Type II errors for the 120-of-200 test above, in context.
A multiple-regression coefficient is \(-0.290\) percentage points per €100,000, with SE 0.058 and a large \(df\). Calculate its t statistic and approximate 95% interval, and interpret the row.
A coefficient estimate is economically negligible but has \(p<0.001\). Explain how both facts can be true.
State two reasons the regression preview cannot support a causal conclusion.







Check your answers






The SE is \(14/\sqrt{49}=2\), so \(t=3/2=1.50\) with \(df=48\); the two-sided p-value is about 0.14. Do not reject the zero mean-difference null at 5% — which is not evidence that the difference is zero.
Type I: concluding the population success proportion differs from 0.50 when it equals 0.50. Type II: failing to detect a genuine specified difference from 0.50.
\(t=-0.290/0.058=-5.00\). With a large \(df\), the 95% interval is approximately \(-0.290\pm1.96(0.058)=(-0.404,\,-0.176)\) percentage points per €100,000. Holding the model’s other predictors fixed, an additional €100,000 requested is associated with between about 0.18 and 0.40 percentage points less fitted equity; reject the zero-coefficient null.
A very large sample or low noise makes the SE tiny, so even a negligible coefficient sits many SEs from zero. Precision does not confer importance.
Season was not randomly assigned, and omitted factors, selection, reverse direction, or measurement error can all remain.






One-sided reasoning (10 minutes)
Lecture 9’s equity-gap test gave \(t=-2.91\) with \(df=99\).

State all three p-values: two-sided, left-sided (\(H_1:\delta<0\)), and right-sided (\(H_1:\delta>0\)).
Which of the three alternatives would have been legitimate to pre-specify, and what determines that?
A classmate, seeing the negative estimate, switches to the left-sided alternative “because it fits the data.” What exactly is wrong?







Check your answers






Two-sided: about 0.0045. Left-sided: about 0.0023 (the single left tail beyond \(-2.91\)). Right-sided: about 0.9977 (everything to the right of \(-2.91\)).
Any of the three — provided it was fixed before inspecting the sample and follows from the research question. Legitimacy is about timing and motivation, not about which alternative is “correct.”
Choosing the tail after seeing the estimate means the 5% rejection mass would follow the data to whichever side the noise landed, so the true Type I error rate is doubled to about 10%. The smaller p-value is bought by an invalid procedure. Course convention: two-sided, always, on the exam.






Spaced review: one item each from Lectures 9 and 5 (10 minutes)

(Lecture 9.) A 95% confidence interval for a mean gap is \((0.4,\,5.2)\) units. State the 5% two-sided test decision without computing, and name one thing the interval reports that the decision does not.
(Lecture 5.) In the full file, the correlation between season and initial equity offered is about \(-0.42\). Interpret this number in one sentence, and state one claim it cannot support.







Check your answers






The interval excludes zero, so the matched two-sided test rejects \(H_0:\delta=0\) at 5%. The interval additionally shows direction, plausible magnitude (0.4 to 5.2 units), and precision.
Season and offered equity have a moderate negative linear association: later-season pitches tend to offer less equity. It cannot support a causal claim — nothing assigned pitches to seasons, and other factors changed over time.






Worked exam interpretation (10 minutes)
Question (Mock Exam Q5 pattern). In a simple random sample of 400 former accelerator participants, 232 had launched a trading venture within one year; a two-sided test of \(H_0:p=0.50\) is planned. The same study fits a regression of monthly revenue (thousands of euros) on weekly mentoring hours; one row of the output is:
                 Estimate  Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)  95% CI
mentoring_hours     0.80       0.25       3.20     0.0016  [0.31, 1.29]
Complete the proportion test at 5% (a large-sample 95% interval for \(p\) is \((0.532,\,0.628)\)), define a Type I error for it, name two power levers that hold \(\alpha\) fixed, and interpret the regression row without causal language.






Check a model answer





Under \(H_0\), \(np_0=n(1-p_0)=200\ge 10\). \(\hat p=232/400=0.58\), \(\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/400}=0.025\), and \(z=0.08/0.025=3.20\) with two-sided p-value about 0.0014: reject \(H_0\); the frame launch proportion differs from 50%, plausibly between 53.2% and 62.8% — the interval excludes 0.50, agreeing with the test. A Type I error would be concluding the launch proportion differs from 50% when it equals 50%. With \(\alpha\) fixed, power rises with a larger sample or lower outcome variability (or a larger true gap, though that is not chosen). The regression row: each additional weekly mentoring hour is associated with 0.80 thousand euros more fitted monthly revenue; \(t=0.80/0.25=3.20\), \(p=0.0016\), and the interval \((0.31,\,1.29)\) excludes zero, so reject \(H_0:\beta=0\). Mentoring hours were not randomly assigned, so this is an association, not a causal effect.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture — or any business you know well. Name one yes-or-no claim you will realistically have to defend with data (our conversion rate beats the sector’s 3%; our average order exceeds the break-even basket), and write two sentences: first state it as a two-sided zero-contrast test and say which of the two errors would be more costly for you and why, then name the one power lever you could actually pull before your next pitch.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “My claim: our conversion rate differs from the sector’s 3% — \(H_0\!: p = 0.03\) against a two-sided alternative. A false alarm is the costlier error, because I would sign a bigger kitchen lease on an effect that is not real; the one power lever I can pull before the next pitch is sample size, by running the tasting stand two more weeks.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to draft the seven-step workflow for your claim and challenge your choice of the more costly error.

Continue to Tutorial 4: Inference and tests against zero.
Formula sheet: Lecture 10 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 15 and 16.

title: Tutorial 4: Inference and tests against zero
text:
In class
Attempt every task before opening its answer. Every conclusion must name the parameter, units, population, direction, and evidence limit.
All tasks use the reproducible seed-123 sample of 100 and the equity gap, built exactly as in Lectures 7 and 9:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]
pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp <- pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct - 15


Task 1 — Mean contrast
For the reproducible sample, define
\[
D=\text{initial equity offered}-15.
\]

Calculate \(\bar d\), \(s_d\), the SE, and the degrees of freedom.
Construct a 95% interval for \(\delta=E[D]\).
Test \(H_0:\delta=0\) against \(H_1:\delta\ne0\).
Explain why the interval and test agree.
Explain why the critical value comes from qt(0.975, df = 99) rather than qnorm(0.975).







Check your answer






d <- pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp
n <- length(d)
d_bar <- mean(d)
s_d <- sd(d)
se_d <- s_d / sqrt(n)
critical <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)
ci_d <- d_bar + c(-1, 1) * critical * se_d
t_value <- d_bar / se_d
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = n - 1)

c(estimate = d_bar, sd = s_d, se = se_d, df = n - 1,
  lower = ci_d[1], upper = ci_d[2],
  t = t_value, p_value = p_value)

    estimate           sd           se           df        lower        upper 
-2.240000000  7.707886555  0.770788656 99.000000000 -3.769411916 -0.710588084 
           t      p_value 
-2.906114385  0.004515396 


\(\bar d=-2.24\), \(s_d=7.7079\), \(SE=0.7708\), and \(df=99\). The 95% interval is approximately \((-3.77,\,-0.71)\). The statistic is \(t=-2.906\) and the two-sided p-value about 0.0045, so reject the zero-gap null. The interval excludes zero because it uses the same t model and SE as the test. The critical value is a t quantile because \(\sigma\) was estimated by \(s_d\); with \(df=99\) the value 1.984 is only slightly above the normal 1.96, but the t choice is the correct procedure.





Task 2 — Proportion contrast
Define \(\delta_p=p-0.50\), where \(p\) is the finite-frame deal proportion.

Estimate \(\delta_p\).
Perform a two-sided large-sample z-test against zero.
Construct the course’s large-sample 95% interval for \(p\) and translate it into an interval for \(\delta_p\).
State why the test and interval SEs differ.







Check your answer






n <- nrow(pitch_sample)
phat <- mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)
p0 <- 0.50
delta_hat <- phat - p0

null_se <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
z_value <- delta_hat / null_se
p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_value))

estimated_se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
ci_p <- phat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * estimated_se
ci_delta <- ci_p - p0

c(phat = phat, estimated_gap = delta_hat,
  z = z_value, p_value = p_value)

         phat estimated_gap             z       p_value 
  0.640000000   0.140000000   2.800000000   0.005110261 

c(proportion_lower = ci_p[1], proportion_upper = ci_p[2],
  gap_lower = ci_delta[1], gap_upper = ci_delta[2])

proportion_lower proportion_upper        gap_lower        gap_upper 
         0.54592          0.73408          0.04592          0.23408 


\(\hat p=0.64\), so \(\widehat\delta_p=0.14\). Under the null, \(SE_0=0.05\), \(z=2.80\), and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. Reject the zero-gap null. The proportion interval is approximately \((0.546,\,0.734)\), corresponding to a gap interval \((0.046,\,0.234)\). The test calculates variation under \(p_0\) — how surprising the sample is in the null’s world — while the interval estimates it with \(\hat p\), making no null assumption.





Task 3 — Read a regression coefficient row
Suppose a model of initial equity offered reports:











Predictor
Estimate
SE
t
p-value
95% interval




Amount requested, per $100,000
-0.290
0.058
-5.00
<0.001
(-0.403, -0.177)




State the tested hypotheses.
Explain every number in units.
Give the statistical conclusion at 5%.
State two claims the row cannot justify.







Check your answer





The test is \(H_0:\beta_{ask}=0\) against \(H_1:\beta_{ask}\ne0\). The estimate says that another $100,000 requested is associated with 0.290 percentage points less fitted initial equity, holding the model’s other predictors fixed. The SE measures sampling uncertainty in the same coefficient units. The statistic is \(-0.290/0.058=-5.00\). The p-value is below 0.001, and the 95% interval excludes zero, so reject the zero-coefficient null. The row alone does not establish causality or show that the model’s assumptions hold.





Task 4 — Errors and power
For Task 3:

describe a Type I error;
describe a Type II error;
state how a larger sample affects SE and power;
explain why raising \(\alpha\) is a trade-off rather than a free gain.







Check your answer





A Type I error is concluding that the population-model ask coefficient differs from zero when it equals zero. A Type II error is failing to reject zero when a specified non-zero coefficient is true. A larger independent sample usually reduces the SE and raises power. Raising \(\alpha\) also raises power, but it increases the Type I error probability by exactly the same mechanism: a wider rejection region catches more of everything.





Task 5 — One-sided alternatives and the exam convention
Task 1 gave \(t=-2.906\) with \(df=99\) and a two-sided p-value of about 0.0045.

Calculate the p-values for the pre-specified one-sided alternatives \(H_1:\delta<0\) and \(H_1:\delta>0\).
A student who saw the negative estimate first proposes to report the left-sided p-value “since the direction is now known.” Explain the error.
State the course’s exam convention and one reason behind it.







Check your answer





Left-sided: \(P(T_{99}\le-2.906)\approx0.0023\), the single left tail. Right-sided: \(P(T_{99}\ge-2.906)\approx0.9977\). Choosing the tail after inspecting the estimate lets the 5% rejection mass follow the data to whichever side the noise landed, which doubles the true Type I error rate to about 10%; the alternative must be fixed by the research question before the sample is examined. Exam convention: all tests are two-sided, both because business questions usually make either direction relevant and because the convention removes the temptation of tail-picking.





Task 6 — Repair the conclusion
Critique:

The coefficient is significant, so asking for more money causes founders to offer less equity, and there is less than a 0.1% chance that the null is true.







Check your answer





The p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and significance does not establish causality. A defensible conclusion reports a negative adjusted association, its magnitude and interval, the evidence against a zero coefficient under the model, and the observational design and assumption limits.
