title: Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
text:
Before class
Total preparation time: about 30 minutes.
Reactivate the recipes (5 minutes). With the Basic formula sheet open, write from memory the general 95% confidence interval recipe and the two-sided test of a benchmark value. Today both recipes return, applied to a regression slope.
Classify (5 minutes). For a useful model, decide whether each quantity should be relatively small or relatively large: SSE, SSR, \(R^2\). Commit to your three answers; the lecture defines all three quantities precisely.
R warm-up (10 minutes). The standing warm-up: rebuild the Lecture 1 model and extract its coefficient table. Bring the table to class — today’s first hour reads it line by line:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1)
deals$ask_1k <- deals$ask_amount_usd / 1000
deals$deal_1k <- deals$deal_amount_usd / 1000
deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
summary(deal_model)$coefficients
If squared terms, ratios, or the interval recipe feel rusty, review Mathematics Refresher: squares, proportions, and standardisation.

title: Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
text:
Video preparation (10 minutes) Watch Stanford Statistical Learning 3.4 Some Important Questions. Focus on the questions “Is there a relationship?” and “How accurately can we predict the response?” All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.








Check your preparation





Interval: \(\text{estimate} \pm (\text{multiplier}) \times
\text{standard error}\), with the multiplier close to 1.96 for large samples. Test: \(t = (\text{estimate} - \text{benchmark})/\text{standard error}\), compared with a t distribution; small p-values are evidence against the benchmark.










Check your preparation





For a useful model, SSE should be relatively small, SSR relatively large, and \(R^2\) relatively large. These are comparisons to total outcome variation, not universal cut-offs.

title: Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question — with the warm-up coefficient table on screen.

Stanford explanation (review): 3.4 Some Important Questions.


How precisely do we know the slope?
The warm-up construction once more, so every object on this page is built in the open:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1)
deals$ask_1k <- deals$ask_amount_usd / 1000
deals$deal_1k <- deals$deal_amount_usd / 1000
deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
summary(deal_model)$coefficients

            Estimate Std. Error  t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 27.57097 7.24074969  3.80775  1.499641e-04
ask_1k       1.00851 0.01820567 55.39538 4.161677e-289


Lecture 1 read only the first column. The other three columns — and the interval R computes from them — are the pentad from QM Basic, returning unchanged. Nothing in this table is new; only the quantity being estimated is:








Pentad ingredient
Where it sits
For the ask–deal slope




estimate
Estimate column
\(b_1 = 1.0085\)


standard error
Std. Error column
\(\operatorname{SE}(b_1) = 0.0182\)


t value
t value column
\(t = 55.4\)


p-value
Pr(>|t|) column
\(< 0.001\)


confidence interval
confint()
computed below



The standard error answers the pentad’s standing question, now about a slope: if we could redraw the sample, how much would \(b_1\) wobble? The estimated slope 1.0085 came from these 882 deals; a different set of deals would give a slightly different line. The SE of 0.0182 — in the slope’s own units, $1,000 of deal per $1,000 of ask — estimates the size of that sampling wobble under the Lecture 2 model conditions.
Degrees of freedom. The interval multiplier comes from a t distribution with \(n - 2 = 882 - 2 = 880\) degrees of freedom. The subtraction is the same bookkeeping as in QM Basic: estimating the intercept and the slope uses two pieces of information before any is left over to estimate the residual spread. (With \(k\) slopes plus an intercept, the residual degrees of freedom become \(n - k - 1\); that general form matters from Lecture 4 onwards.) At 880 degrees of freedom, the multiplier \(t_{0.975,\,880} = 1.963\) is indistinguishable in practice from the familiar 1.96.

Example 19.1 (Worked example: the slope interval by hand) Everything comes from the coefficient table: \(b_1 = 1.0085\), \(\operatorname{SE}(b_1) = 0.0182\), multiplier \(\approx 1.96\).
\[
b_1 \pm t_{0.975,\,880}\operatorname{SE}(b_1)
= 1.0085 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0182
= 1.0085 \pm 0.0357
= (0.973,\; 1.044).
\]
In words: under the model conditions, the data are consistent with a population slope between about $973 and $1,044 of agreed amount per $1,000 requested. The interval’s endpoints carry the slope’s units — that is the pentad rule that the estimate, SE, and interval share units, while t and the p-value are unit-free.
R agrees:

confint(deal_model)

                 2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 13.3598133 41.782122
ask_1k       0.9727782  1.044241



The interval describes sampling uncertainty under the model conditions. It does not include uncertainty from selection into televised pitches, the decision to analyse only on-air deals, or measurement choices — no formula widens an interval for a flawed design.


The t-test against zero
The standard significance test asks whether the data are consistent with no linear association:
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\beta_1\ne0,
\qquad
t=\frac{b_1-0}{\operatorname{SE}(b_1)}.
\]
By hand, once: \(t = 1.0085 / 0.0182 \approx 55.4\). An estimate 55 standard errors from zero is astronomically far into the tail of a t distribution. Live verification, computing the p-value exactly as QM Basic did:

coef_table <- summary(deal_model)$coefficients
b1 <- coef_table["ask_1k", "Estimate"]
se_b1 <- coef_table["ask_1k", "Std. Error"]
t_value <- b1 / se_b1
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df.residual(deal_model))
c(estimate = b1, standard_error = se_b1,
  t_statistic = t_value, p_value = p_value)

      estimate standard_error    t_statistic        p_value 
  1.008510e+00   1.820567e-02   5.539538e+01  4.161677e-289 


What the tiny p-value does say: if the population slope were zero and the model conditions held, a sample slope this far from zero would essentially never occur — strong evidence against a zero linear association in this selected sample.
What it does not say, one line each:

it does not say the model is correctly specified — Lecture 2’s fan and influential pitches stand as the permanent caveat under this table;
it does not say the association is large or important — with 882 observations, even tiny slopes can earn tiny p-values;
it does not say that requesting more causes a larger deal — no test statistic repairs an observational design.







Check: the p-value is 4×10-289. Is this slope therefore trustworthy?





No. The p-value measures distance from zero in standard-error units, and the standard error was computed under the classical conditions — constant error variance and independent rows among them. Lecture 2 showed the residual fan and the handful of pitches that steer the fit, so this particular SE rests on doubtful ground. “Significant” means the data are inconsistent with a zero slope, not that 0.0182 is the right measure of wobble.





Decomposing variation
The second part of the driving question — how much does the line explain? — needs a benchmark. Without a predictor, the best single prediction for every deal is the mean agreed amount \(\bar y\). Regression is useful to the extent that the fitted values \(\widehat y_i\) improve on that flat prediction.
For each observation, the total deviation from the mean splits exactly into an explained part and a residual part, as Figure 19.1 shows for one point:
\[
\underbrace{y_i-\bar y}_{\text{total}}
=
\underbrace{(\widehat y_i-\bar y)}_{\text{explained by the line}}
+
\underbrace{(y_i-\widehat y_i)}_{\text{residual}}.
\]


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
x_d <- c(1, 2.2, 3.4, 4.6, 5.8, 7.0, 8.2)
y_d <- 1 + 0.8 * x_d + c(1.3, -1.5, 0.9, -0.8, 1.6, -1.2, 0.4)
fit_d <- lm(y_d ~ x_d)
decomp_df <- data.frame(x = x_d, y = y_d)
i <- 5
xh <- x_d[i]; yh <- y_d[i]; fh <- fitted(fit_d)[i]; mh <- mean(y_d)

ggplot(decomp_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mh, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit_d)[1], slope = coef(fit_d)[2],
              colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("segment", x = xh + 0.55, xend = xh + 0.55, y = mh, yend = yh,
           colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("segment", x = xh, xend = xh, y = mh, yend = fh,
           colour = "#009E73", linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("segment", x = xh, xend = xh, y = fh, yend = yh,
           colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  annotate("text", x = xh + 1.25, y = (mh + yh) / 2,
           label = "y[i] - bar(y)", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = xh - 0.85, y = (mh + fh) / 2,
           label = "hat(y)[i] - bar(y)", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = xh - 0.75, y = (fh + yh) / 2 + 0.15,
           label = "y[i] - hat(y)[i]", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#0072B2", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.0, y = mh - 0.45, label = "bar(y)",
           parse = TRUE, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.4, y = coef(fit_d)[1] + coef(fit_d)[2] * 9.4 + 0.5,
           label = "fitted line", hjust = 1,
           colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 9.6), ylim = c(0, 9.6)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor X", y = "Outcome Y") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 19.1: One observation’s total deviation from the mean of Y splits into the part the fitted line explains and the residual. Squaring and summing over all observations gives SST = SSR + SSE.





Square each piece and sum over all observations. For ordinary least squares with an intercept, the cross-terms cancel and the identity holds exactly:
\[
\underbrace{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\text{SST: total}}
=
\underbrace{\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\text{SSR: explained}}
+
\underbrace{\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2}_{\text{SSE: residual}}.
\]
Live, on the deal model, with the identity checked:

y <- deals$deal_1k
yhat <- fitted(deal_model)

SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
SSR <- sum((yhat - mean(y))^2)
SSE <- sum((y - yhat)^2)

c(SST = SST, SSR = SSR, SSE = SSE, check = SSR + SSE)

      SST       SSR       SSE     check 
103509324  80441122  23068202 103509324 


The units are squared thousands of dollars, so the raw magnitudes (around \(10^8\)) mean little on their own — the sums of squares matter only relative to each other, which is exactly what the next section computes.

Example 19.2 (Worked example: from SST and SSE to SSR and R²) A regression output reports \(\text{SST} = 500\) and \(\text{SSE} = 125\). Find SSR and \(R^2\).
By the identity, \(\text{SSR} = \text{SST} - \text{SSE} = 500 - 125 = 375\). Then
\[
R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = \frac{375}{500} = 0.75
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{125}{500} = 0.75.
\]
The fitted values account for 75% of the observed sample variation in the outcome; 25% remains as residual variation around the line. In class, the one-click Mentimeter check on this calculation is posed right before the break.



R²: what 0.777 means — and four things it is not
The general definition, applied to the live numbers:
\[
R^2=\frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}
=1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}.
\]

c(
  manual = 1 - SSE / SST,
  from_R = summary(deal_model)$r.squared,
  correlation_squared = cor(deals$ask_1k, deals$deal_1k)^2
)

             manual              from_R correlation_squared 
          0.7771389           0.7771389           0.7771389 


Here \(R^2 \approx 0.777\): about 77.7% of the observed sample variation in agreed on-air deal amounts, among deal records, is explained by the linear association with the amount requested. The third number above shows a simple-regression bonus fact: with an intercept, \(R^2 = r_{XY}^2\), the squared correlation. Squaring discards the sign, so inspect the slope or correlation for direction.
\(R^2\) is one of the most misquoted numbers in applied work. Four things it is not, each with a wrong sentence corrected. The first two are worked here; the last two are yours.
Not the percentage of correct predictions. Wrong: “The model predicts 77.7% of deal amounts correctly.” Corrected: the model explains 77.7% of the variation in deal amounts; individual predictions can still miss by hundreds of thousands of dollars (the residual standard error is about $162,000).
Not proof that the assumptions hold. Wrong: “With \(R^2\) this high, the model is clearly well specified.” Corrected: \(R^2\) measures fit, not validity — Lecture 2 found a residual fan and influential pitches in this very model, and 0.777 is silent about both.






Try it: correct the last two wrong sentences





In class this is the pair task. Correct each sentence in one line, as above.
Sentence 3 (you). “Asking explains 78% of the deal, so raising your ask will raise your deal.”
Sentence 4 (you). “The model will explain 77.7% of deal-amount variation in next year’s pitches too.”






Check your answers





Sentence 3 claims causation: \(R^2\) describes an association among observed deals; requests were not randomly assigned, and nothing in a fit statistic says what would happen if a founder changed their ask. Sentence 4 claims out-of-sample performance: \(R^2\) is computed on this sample; a new season, a different selection of pitches, or a changed negotiation culture can all lower it. In-sample fit is evidence about these 882 records, not a guarantee for the next 882.








The overall F-test
The last part of the driving question: is the model useful at all, compared with predicting \(\bar y\) for everyone? For a regression with \(k\) predictors, the overall usefulness test is
\[
H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=0
\]
against the alternative that at least one slope is non-zero. The statistic is
\[
F=\frac{\text{SSR}/k}{\text{SSE}/(n-k-1)}.
\]
Read the ratio the way it is built: the numerator is explained variation per predictor; the denominator is residual variation per residual degree of freedom. F asks how many times more explanation the model buys, per coefficient spent, than leftover noise would suggest. Values near 1 are what pure noise delivers; large values are evidence that the predictors jointly matter.
The whole lecture now sits in one printed block — read summary() from top to bottom in this order: (1) formula and analysis sample, (2) coefficient estimates and units, (3) standard errors, t statistics, and p-values, (4) residual scale, (5) \(R^2\) and adjusted \(R^2\), (6) the overall F-test — and (7) everything the table does not print: assumptions and design limits.

summary(deal_model)


Call:
lm(formula = deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-434.38  -30.12  -28.85  -28.21 2821.15 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 27.57097    7.24075   3.808  0.00015 ***
ask_1k       1.00851    0.01821  55.395  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 161.9 on 880 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7771,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7769 
F-statistic:  3069 on 1 and 880 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The output reports \(F \approx 3069\) on 1 and 880 degrees of freedom, with a p-value too small to print meaningfully. Rejecting the null says the model with requested amount fits better than an intercept-only model, under the inferential conditions.
In simple regression, F and t answer the same question. With one predictor and a two-sided alternative, \(H_0:\beta_1 = 0\) is the entire joint null, and
\[
F = t^2.
\]

t_slope <- summary(deal_model)$coefficients["ask_1k", "t value"]
f_model <- unname(summary(deal_model)$fstatistic["value"])
c(t_squared = t_slope^2, F = f_model)

t_squared         F 
 3068.648  3068.648 


Both equal about 3069. This equivalence dies in multiple regression, where the F-test evaluates several slopes jointly while each t-test evaluates one — Lecture 5 builds a genuine joint test on exactly that difference.


Usefulness has more than one meaning
“Is the model useful?” has at least four distinct readings, and a model can pass one while failing another:

Statistically non-zero slope, low \(R^2\). A loyalty-programme analysis on 400,000 customers finds a reliably positive effect of mailings on spending — real, precisely estimated, and explaining 1% of spending variation. Useful for a mass decision, useless for predicting any one customer.
High \(R^2\), poor causal interpretation. Store revenue regressed on staff count fits beautifully — because both track store size. Hiring more staff at a small store will not produce a big store’s revenue.
Good in-sample fit, fragile out-of-sample prediction. A travel-demand model fitted on 2015–2019 data explained bookings superbly and collapsed in 2020. In-sample \(R^2\) never promised stability.
Accurate predictions, no structural story. A black-box model may forecast weekly orders extremely well while its coefficients support no explanation of why — fine for stocking decisions, useless for designing a price change.

Always align the evaluation with the goal: explanation, prediction, or decision support.

Optional: robust standard errors Heteroskedasticity-consistent, or robust, standard errors relax the constant-variance assumption when computing uncertainty. The fitted coefficients remain the ordinary least-squares values; only the estimated SEs (and hence t values, p-values, and intervals) change. Given Lecture 2’s residual fan, they are a natural upgrade for this model:

# Run this if these packages are available in the course R environment
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

coeftest(deal_model, vcov. = vcovHC(deal_model, type = "HC1"))

They fix exactly one thing: a misspecified conditional error variance. They do not repair non-linearity, omitted-variable bias, dependence across rows, influential data errors, or non-random selection. A robust SE on a biased slope is a precise measurement of the wrong quantity.


What a precise slope and a high R² can and cannot say
Every number this lecture produced — the SE of 0.0182, the interval \((0.973, 1.044)\), the p-value, \(R^2 = 0.777\), \(F \approx 3069\) — is computed under the model conditions of Lecture 2, and the diagnostics there flagged two of them: the residual spread grows with deal size, and a handful of extreme pitches steer the fit. So the classical SE (and everything built from it) rests on a doubtful variance assumption, and both the slope and \(R^2\) are partly the work of a few identifiable records. Beyond that, the sample is on-air deals only — selection travels with every estimate — and none of today’s statistics moves the association any closer to a causal claim. Precision and fit are internal report cards, not external validation.



Answering the driving question
Precisely, substantially, and yes — with conditions. The slope 1.0085 has standard error 0.0182, so the 95% interval \((0.973, 1.044)\) pins the association down to within about seven cents per dollar asked; the t-test rejects a zero slope beyond any doubt (\(t \approx 55.4\)). The line explains 77.7% of the variation in agreed amounts, and the overall F-test (\(F \approx 3069\)) confirms the model beats a flat mean. Every one of those statements is conditional on the Lecture 2 diagnostics — the fan and the influential pitches — and none of them is causal.
Next: Tutorial 1 rehearses Lectures 1–3 in exam format and in TestVision style: fit a model in R, diagnose it, and defend its coefficients with intervals, tests, and \(R^2\) — the complete simple-regression pipeline you now own. Bring your attempts; the session starts from them.

title: Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 70 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

Why are the residual degrees of freedom \(n-2\) in simple regression?
Which pentad quantities share the slope’s units, and which are unit-free?
What do SST, SSR, and SSE measure, and how are they related?
Why is \(R^2\) between 0 and 1 in an OLS model with an intercept?
What is the null hypothesis of the overall F-test, and why does \(F=t^2\) in simple regression?
What single problem do robust standard errors address?







Check your answers






Two coefficients — intercept and slope — are estimated before residual variation can be measured, using up two pieces of information.
The estimate, its SE, and the interval endpoints share the slope’s units; the t statistic and p-value are unit-free.
Total, explained (fitted), and residual sample variation in the outcome; \(\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}\) for OLS with an intercept.
SSE is non-negative and no larger than SST, so \(1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}\) lies between 0 and 1.
All population slope coefficients are zero. With one predictor that is the same hypothesis as the two-sided slope t-test, and \(F=t^2\).
Misspecified (non-constant) conditional error variance — nothing else.






From worked to faded: an interval for a new row (15 minutes)
Re-read the worked slope interval (Example 19.1). Then build the interval for the intercept row of the same table.
Step 1 (given). From the coefficient table: estimate \(27.571\), standard error \(7.241\), degrees of freedom \(880\), multiplier \(\approx 1.96\).
Step 2 (you). Compute the 95% interval.
Step 3 (you). Interpret it in one sentence — and say why this particular interval has little standalone business value (Lecture 1 told you).






Check your answer





\(27.571 \pm 1.96 \times 7.241 = 27.571 \pm 14.19 = (13.4,\; 41.8)\), in $1,000s — R’s exact answer is \((13.36, 41.78)\). Under the model conditions, the data are consistent with a population intercept between about $13,400 and $41,800. But the intercept is the fitted mean at a request of zero, outside the observed range of asks, so the interval is mathematically sound and substantively unhelpful.



Then the unassisted set:

A study reports a coefficient of 2.40 with standard error 0.80 in a large sample. Compute the t statistic, decide the 5% two-sided test against zero, and give the 95% interval.
Interpret \(R^2=0.20\) without calling the model “80% wrong.”
A model has \(k=3\), \(n=104\), SSR = 300, and SSE = 500. Calculate F.
Explain why adding a predictor cannot increase the in-sample SSE in OLS.







Check your answers






\(t = 2.40/0.80 = 3\); reject at 5% (well beyond 1.96). Interval: \(2.40 \pm 1.96 \times 0.80 = (0.83,\; 3.97)\).
The fitted values explain 20% of observed outcome variation; 80% remains as residual variation around the fitted line. Nothing is “wrong” — the model’s predictions are simply far from individual outcomes.
\(F=(300/3)/(500/(104-3-1))=100/5=20\).
The expanded model can reproduce the old fit by setting the new slope to zero, so least squares cannot end at a larger minimum SSE.






Practice: the full pipeline on equity and season (20 minutes)
Fit equity_offered_pct ~ season on all 1,441 pitches. Report the slope’s 95% confidence interval, the t-test against zero, \(R^2\), and the overall F-test — then write a 120-word conclusion that separates estimate, uncertainty, fit, and scope.






Check a model answer






sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
equity_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks)
summary(equity_model)$coefficients

              Estimate Std. Error   t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 20.4565874 0.46442667  44.04697 4.922706e-269
season      -0.8241241 0.04752298 -17.34159  2.514546e-61

confint(equity_model)

                 2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 19.5455616 21.3676132
season      -0.9173458 -0.7309023

c(r_squared = summary(equity_model)$r.squared,
  F = unname(summary(equity_model)$fstatistic["value"]))

  r_squared           F 
  0.1728605 300.7308055 


A complete conclusion reports: one later season is associated with about 0.824 percentage points less initial equity offered (SE 0.048); the 95% interval \((-0.917, -0.731)\) excludes zero and the t-test rejects a zero slope (\(t\approx-17.3\), p \(<\) 0.001); season explains about 17.3% of observed equity-offer variation, and the overall F-test (\(F\approx300.7 = t^2\)) rejects the intercept-only model. Scope: an observational time trend among recorded pitches — not a causal effect of season, and the classical SEs assume the Lecture 2 conditions.





Spaced review: one diagnostics item from Lecture 2 (5 minutes)
The residual-versus-fitted plot of the deal model fans out to the right. Which of today’s printed numbers does that pattern undermine most directly, and why?






Check your answer





The classical standard error 0.0182 — and with it the t statistic, p-value, and confidence interval built from it. The classical SE formula assumes one common error variance \(\sigma^2\); a fan says the conditional variance grows with the fitted value, so the stated precision is doubtful. Robust SEs address exactly this one problem; they repair nothing else.





Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question (mock exam Question 3 pattern). A model of venture sales growth (percentage points) on marketing spending (€10,000s), fitted on \(n = 102\) ventures, reports a slope of 1.38 with standard error 0.46, \(R^2 = 0.083\), and \(F = 9.0\). Build the 95% interval for the slope, decide the 5% test against zero, verify the F statistic from the t statistic, and state in one sentence what the low \(R^2\) does and does not imply.






Check a model answer





\(t = 1.38/0.46 = 3.0\); with \(df = 100\) the multiplier is about 1.98, so the interval is \(1.38 \pm 1.98\times0.46 \approx (0.47,\; 2.29)\) percentage points per €10,000. The interval excludes zero, so the two-sided 5% test rejects \(H_0:\beta_1=0\); consistently, \(F = t^2 = 9.0\). The low \(R^2\) says marketing spending explains about 8% of growth variation — predictions for individual ventures will be poor — but it does not undo the evidence that the association is non-zero, and neither number makes the association causal.





From the reading ladder (10 minutes)
The reading ladder returns to Tierney & Farmer (2002) — the paper whose correlation table you read in Basic Lecture 5. This time find a regression table and pick one coefficient row. Apply today’s pentad reading: the estimate and its sign, the reported SE or significance marker, what null hypothesis the star implicitly tests, and what the careful one-sentence interpretation is. Then find the reported \(R^2\) (or change in \(R^2\)) and say in one sentence what it does — and does not — tell you about the model’s usefulness.






Check your approach





Your sentence should name the outcome, the predictor’s units or scale, and “holding the other included variables fixed”, and the significance star should translate to “a t-test against zero rejects at the marked level” — nothing more. If the \(R^2\) sentence avoided both “the model is good” and “the model is bad” and instead said what share of outcome variation the predictors account for in this sample, you read the table the way this course intends.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture — or any business you know well — and one regression you might run on its data. Write two sentences: first say which you would rather have for your next decision, a precise slope (narrow interval) or a high \(R^2\), and why; then name the usefulness meaning from today’s four-case list that matters most for that decision. There is no wrong answer; the point is noticing that precision and fit answer different questions.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “For setting next month’s ad budget I would take a precise slope over a high \(R^2\): I need to know what an extra €100 buys, even if week-to-week orders stay noisy. That is the levers meaning of usefulness — predicting individual weeks matters less to me than the payoff of an input I control.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to invent a business model with a significant slope and a low \(R^2\) and challenge you to say what the model is still useful for.

Continue to Tutorial 1: Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness.
Formula sheet: Lecture 3 formulas.
For a more formal treatment, see James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Sections 3.1.2–3.1.3, and Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 19–20.

Before class

The standing routine for each task is the same — the TA states the task, pairs work on it first for a few minutes with AI use allowed, and the solution is then discussed in plenary, starting from the pair attempts.
One note on the order. The tasks run in course order: Tasks 1–2 rest on Lecture 1, Task 3 on Lecture 2, and Tasks 4–5 on yesterday’s Lecture 3. This is deliberate — the tutorial meets the day after Lecture 3, so you warm up on settled material before testing what you learned yesterday.

title: Tutorial 1: Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness
text:
In class
Attempt each task in R before opening the answer. A complete written answer names the sample, shows the calculation, reports values with units, interprets in context, and states an important model or design boundary.
All tasks use the Shark Tank teaching file and the running money unit of thousands of dollars. Build the analysis data once — this is the same construction as Lectures 1–3:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1)
deals$ask_1k <- deals$ask_amount_usd / 1000
deals$deal_1k <- deals$deal_amount_usd / 1000


Task 1 — Fit and interpret (Lecture 1)
Fit deal_1k ~ ask_1k among the on-air deal records. Report the sample, the fitted equation, the slope interpretation with units, and the intercept limitation.






Check your answer






deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
coef(deal_model)

(Intercept)      ask_1k 
   27.57097     1.00851 


Among the 882 pitches with an on-air deal, the fitted equation is \(\widehat y = 27.571 + 1.0085x\), with both variables in $1,000s. One additional $1,000 requested is associated with about $1,008.50 more in fitted agreed amount. A zero request is outside the observed range, so the intercept (about $27,600) lacks a useful standalone business interpretation.





Task 2 — Fitted value and residual (Lecture 1)
A pitch requested $500,000 and agreed $450,000.

Calculate its fitted value.
Calculate its residual.
Interpret the sign of the residual.







Check your answer





With \(x=500\) (in \(1,000s),\)y = 27.571 + 1.0085 $, or about $531,826. The observed \(y = 450\), so \(e = 450 - 531.83 = -81.83\), about \(-\$81{,}826\). The negative sign means this pitch agreed less than the model’s fitted conditional mean for a $500,000 request.

deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
unname(450 - predict(deal_model, newdata = data.frame(ask_1k = 500)))

[1] -81.82589







Task 3 — Diagnostics and influence (Lecture 2)
Produce the residual-versus-fitted plot and the normal Q–Q plot for the Task 1 model.

Name two visible assumption concerns.
Count the standardised residuals beyond \(\pm 3\) and the observations above the \(4/n\) Cook’s distance screen.
State the three-step rule for handling a flagged observation.
Name one assumption these plots cannot assess and what would assess it.







Check your answer






deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1)
plot(fitted(deal_model), residuals(deal_model),
     pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", alpha.f = 0.35),
     bty = "n", xlab = "Fitted agreed amount ($1,000s)",
     ylab = "Residual ($1,000s)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00")
qqnorm(rstandard(deal_model), pch = 16,
       col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#009E73", alpha.f = 0.40),
       bty = "n", main = "", xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile",
       ylab = "Standardised residual")
qqline(rstandard(deal_model), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2)







par(old_par)
c(big_rstandard = sum(abs(rstandard(deal_model)) > 3),
  cooks_flagged = sum(cooks.distance(deal_model) > 4 / nrow(deals)))

big_rstandard cooks_flagged 
           12            21 


Residual spread widens with the fitted value (a fan, challenging constant conditional variance), and the Q–Q plot shows a heavy right tail with several extreme positive residuals (challenging normality and flagging influence). Twelve standardised residuals exceed \(\pm3\) and 21 observations exceed the \(4/n\) Cook’s screen — the most influential pitch asked $150,000 and agreed $3,000,000. The rule: investigate, report, never silently delete. The plots cannot assess independence (or zero conditional mean); those need knowledge of the data collection — for example whether founders or ventures appear in multiple rows.





Task 4 — Coefficient inference (Lecture 3)
Use summary() and confint() on the Task 1 model.

Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) against the two-sided alternative.
Report the 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\), and verify it by hand from the estimate and SE.
Would robust standard errors fix both concerns from Task 3?







Check your answer






deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
summary(deal_model)$coefficients

            Estimate Std. Error  t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 27.57097 7.24074969  3.80775  1.499641e-04
ask_1k       1.00851 0.01820567 55.39538 4.161677e-289

confint(deal_model)

                 2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 13.3598133 41.782122
ask_1k       0.9727782  1.044241


The slope is \(1.0085\) with classical SE \(0.0182\), so \(t = 1.0085/0.0182 \approx 55.4\) on \(880\) degrees of freedom and the p-value is far below 0.001: reject a zero slope. By hand, \(1.0085 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0182 = (0.973,\; 1.044)\), matching confint() — in $1,000s of deal per $1,000 asked. Robust SEs address the unequal variance only; they do not remove influential observations, selection into deals, or a misspecified mean.





Task 5 — R² and F (Lecture 3)

Calculate SST, SSE, SSR, and \(R^2\) manually.
Verify them against summary().
Verify \(F = t^2\).
Write one concluding sentence that does not overclaim.







Check your answer






deal_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = deals)
y <- deals$deal_1k
yhat <- fitted(deal_model)
SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
SSE <- sum((y - yhat)^2)
SSR <- sum((yhat - mean(y))^2)
c(R2_manual = 1 - SSE / SST,
  R2_summary = summary(deal_model)$r.squared,
  F_summary = unname(summary(deal_model)$fstatistic["value"]),
  t_squared = summary(deal_model)$coefficients["ask_1k", "t value"]^2)

   R2_manual   R2_summary    F_summary    t_squared 
   0.7771389    0.7771389 3068.6477368 3068.6477368 


The sums (in squared $1,000s) satisfy \(\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}\), and \(R^2 \approx 0.777\). The overall F statistic is about 3069, equal to the squared slope t statistic, as it must be in simple regression. A sentence that does not overclaim: requested amount explains about 78% of the observed variation in agreed amounts among on-air deals, but this selected observational association — shaped partly by a few influential pitches — is not a causal effect of changing an ask.

title: Tutorial 1: Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness
text:
After class

Timed individual practice — 20 minutes
Fit equity_offered_pct ~ season using all 1,441 records.

Make and read the scatterplot with the fitted line.
Report the fitted equation and units.
Report the slope SE, t statistic, p-value, and 95% interval.
Report \(R^2\) and the overall F-test.
Inspect the residual plots and write a 120-word model conclusion.







Check a model answer





The fitted equation is \(\widehat{equity}=20.457-0.824\,season\): one later season is associated with about 0.824 percentage points less initial equity offered on average. The classical SE is about 0.048, \(t\approx-17.3\), and the p-value is below 0.001; the 95% interval \((-0.917,\,-0.731)\) excludes zero. \(R^2\approx0.173\), so season explains about 17.3% of observed equity-offer variation, and the overall F-test (\(F\approx300.7=t^2\)) reaches the same conclusion as the slope test. The residual plot shows sixteen vertical stripes (season is whole-numbered) with broadly similar spread, and the Q–Q plot a heavy right tail from very high offers. This is an observational time association among recorded pitches, not a causal effect of progressing to a later season.





Check your understanding
Complete from memory:

A residual is …
The slope’s standard error estimates …
A fan in the residual plot challenges …
\(R^2\) is the proportion of …
In simple regression, the overall F statistic equals …







Check your answers






The observed outcome minus the fitted value, \(e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i\).
How much the estimated slope would vary across repeated samples under the model conditions.
Constant conditional variance (homoskedasticity) — and with it the classical standard errors.
Observed sample variation in the outcome explained by the fitted values, \(\text{SSR}/\text{SST}\).
The squared slope t statistic, \(F=t^2\).






Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture — or any business you know well. Imagine the one simple regression you would show an investor (revenue on customers, orders on ad spend), and write two sentences: first name the number from today’s pipeline you would put in the headline — slope, interval, or \(R^2\) — and why, then name the caveat from Task 3 or Task 5 you would be honest about in the footnote. There is no wrong answer; the point is pairing every headline number with its boundary.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “Headline: the slope with its 95% interval — each extra €100 of ads is associated with roughly 12 to 19 more orders — because an investor asks what money buys, and the interval carries the honesty. Footnote: the fan shape in my residual plot means busy weeks are noisier, so that interval leans on an assumption my own diagnostics question.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this tutorial — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: paste your two sentences and ask it to play the sceptical investor.

Continue to Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do.

Before class
Total preparation time: about 30 minutes.
Reactivate (10 minutes). In Lecture 3 you fitted the simple season model and tested its slope. Fit it again, then fit the two-predictor model that adds the requested amount in thousands of dollars, and bring both season coefficients to class:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
coef(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks))
coef(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks))
Predict (5 minutes). Answer the one-click Mentimeter question posted on Canvas before you come to class: once the requested amount is added, will the season coefficient move towards zero, away from zero, or barely move? Think about why the slope might change at all: if the requested amount is associated with both season and offered equity, the simple slope mixes their relationships. Commit to an answer; the lecture resolves it.
If subscripts or multivariable equations feel rusty, review Mathematics Refresher: subscripts and multivariable equations.

title: Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do
text:
In class
The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Your warm-up produced two season coefficients — about \(-0.824\) without the requested amount and \(-0.814\) with it. This lecture explains what the second number means, why the two can differ, and why here they barely do.

More than one predictor

Stanford explanation (review): 3.3 Multiple Linear Regression.

For predictors \(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{ik}\), the model is
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kX_{ik}+\varepsilon_i,
\]
with conditional mean
\[
E[Y_i\mid X_{i1}=x_1,\ldots,X_{ik}=x_k]
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_kx_k.
\]
The coefficient \(\beta_j\) is the expected change in \(Y\) for a one-unit increase in \(X_j\), holding the other included predictors fixed. That phrase must appear in every multiple-regression slope interpretation you write in this course.
It describes a model-based comparison. It does not require that two real pitches exist that are identical on every feature; it compares fitted conditional means at fixed values of the included variables. The model does the holding fixed — the data need not contain twins.


Why coefficients change: a constructed demonstration
Before touching the Shark Tank data, watch the mechanism operate where we control it completely, because we built the data ourselves. Imagine 200 small firms. A single background variable — firm size — drives both advertising spend and revenue. Advertising itself contributes nothing: the revenue line below contains size but no adspend term.

set.seed(42)
n <- 200
size    <- rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2)          # Z: firm size (drives both)
adspend <- 2 + 0.8 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1)    # X: bigger firms spend more
revenue <- 5 + 1.5 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)  # Y: size drives revenue,
demo <- data.frame(revenue, adspend, size)      #    adspend does not
coef(lm(revenue ~ adspend, data = demo))

(Intercept)     adspend 
   5.957361    1.391909 

coef(lm(revenue ~ adspend + size, data = demo))

(Intercept)     adspend        size 
  5.0975426   0.1007622   1.3804961 


The simple slope of adspend is about \(1.39\): strongly positive, and highly significant if you check its t statistic. Yet we know advertising does nothing here. Once size enters the model, the adspend slope collapses to about \(0.10\) with a p-value around \(0.39\) — indistinguishable from the zero we built in. The simple slope was entirely an omitted-variable artefact: adspend earned credit for the size differences it was correlated with.
Figure 21.1 makes the mechanism visible. Larger firms (orange) sit high on both axes; smaller firms (blue) sit low on both. Sliding along the overall cloud from left to right, you move from small firms to large firms — so the simple slope compares different kinds of firms. Within each colour, the cloud is nearly flat: at a given size, spending more is not associated with more revenue.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
n <- 200
size    <- rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2)          # Z: firm size (drives both)
adspend <- 2 + 0.8 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1)    # X: bigger firms spend more
revenue <- 5 + 1.5 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)  # Y: size drives revenue,
demo <- data.frame(revenue, adspend, size)      #    adspend does not
demo$group <- ifelse(demo$size > median(demo$size),
                     "Larger firms (size above median)",
                     "Smaller firms (size below median)")
simple_fit <- lm(revenue ~ adspend, data = demo)

ggplot(demo, aes(x = adspend, y = revenue,
                 colour = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(simple_fit)[1],
              slope = coef(simple_fit)[2],
              colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = max(demo$adspend) - 0.2,
           y = coef(simple_fit)[1] + coef(simple_fit)[2] *
             (max(demo$adspend) - 0.2) - 2.4,
           label = "simple regression line",
           hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Larger firms (size above median)" = "#D55E00",
    "Smaller firms (size below median)" = "#0072B2"
  )) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Larger firms (size above median)" = 17,
    "Smaller firms (size below median)" = 16
  )) +
  labs(x = "Advertising spend (constructed units)",
       y = "Revenue (constructed units)",
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )








Figure 21.1: Constructed data: revenue against advertising spend for 200 simulated firms, coloured by firm size. The overall upward drift comes entirely from size; within a colour group the relationship is nearly flat.





A coefficient changes when an added predictor accounts for variation that the simpler association had absorbed. That is the entire mechanism — and it is why “holding the other included predictors fixed” is not decoration but the substance of the estimate.


The real-data contrast: the season slope barely moves
Now the same comparison on the Shark Tank data. The running money unit from here on is thousands of dollars: ask_1k is the requested amount divided by 1,000, so one unit is $1,000 and 100 units are $100,000 (Lecture 1 showed how a coefficient rescales when the unit changes).

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
m_simple   <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks)
m_adjusted <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks)
c(
  simple           = coef(m_simple)["season"],
  adjusted_for_ask = coef(m_adjusted)["season"]
)

          simple.season adjusted_for_ask.season 
             -0.8241241              -0.8143307 


The season slope moves from about \(-0.824\) to about \(-0.814\): hardly at all. Contrast this with the constructed example, where adjustment destroyed the simple slope. Here, adjusting for the requested amount leaves the season trend essentially intact, so within these data the time story is not a disguised money story.
Read the stability correctly. It is informative: the measured requested amount does not account for the season trend. It is not proof that omitted-variable bias is absent: an unmeasured variable — venture maturity, founder experience, editorial selection — could still play exactly the role size played in the constructed data. Stability with respect to the variables you have says nothing about the variables you do not have.


A three-predictor Shark Tank model
Add a third predictor and fit the model this lecture works with. The outcome is initial equity offered, in percentage points. The predictors are:

season — the season number, 1 to 16;
ask_1k — requested amount in thousands of dollars;
description_words — the number of words in the source’s short description of the business.


equity_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)
summary(equity_model)


Call:
lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, 
    data = sharks)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-15.295  -4.776  -1.283   3.288  82.106 

Coefficients:
                    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       22.0249310  0.8878522  24.807  < 2e-16 ***
season            -0.8361515  0.0509825 -16.401  < 2e-16 ***
ask_1k            -0.0028975  0.0005771  -5.021 5.79e-07 ***
description_words -0.1283379  0.1137527  -1.128    0.259    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.619 on 1437 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1876,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1859 
F-statistic: 110.6 on 3 and 1437 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The fitted equation is approximately
\[
\widehat{equity}
=22.025-0.836\,season-0.0029\,ask_{1k}
-0.128\,description\_words.
\]

The coefficient-interpretation protocol
Use the same five checks every time you interpret a slope:

Estimate and direction: state the fitted change and its sign.
Predictor step and unit: say what a one-unit increase means.
Outcome unit: state the unit in which the outcome changes.
Conditioning: name the other included predictors being held fixed.
Scope: identify the analysed records and say “associated with” unless a research design justifies a causal claim.

The variables in this model use deliberately different units:








Term
A one-unit increase means
Coefficient unit




season
one later season
equity percentage points per season


ask_1k
$1,000 more requested
equity percentage points per $1,000


description_words
one additional word
equity percentage points per word



Applying the protocol to each slope in turn, always among the 1,441 recorded pitches:

Season. At the same requested amount and description length, one later season is associated with about \(0.836\) percentage points less initial equity offered.
Requested amount. At the same season and description length, an additional $1,000 requested is associated with about \(0.0029\) percentage points less initial equity offered. The number is tiny because the unit step is tiny; per additional $100,000 the association is about \(0.29\) percentage points, and its t statistic (about \(-5.0\)) does not depend on the unit chosen.
Description length. At the same season and request, one additional description word is associated with about \(0.128\) percentage points less initial equity offered. This estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero at 5% (p \(\approx\) 0.26). Report the point estimate anyway: “not significant” is not the same as “exactly zero” — the data are simply consistent with a range of values that includes zero.







Check: the season slope was −0.814 with two predictors and −0.836 with three. Contradiction?





No. Each coefficient answers a different conditional question: \(-0.814\) holds only ask_1k fixed; \(-0.836\) holds ask_1k and description_words fixed. Adding a predictor changes what is being held fixed, so the coefficient may shift. Here the shift is small — the same stability, and the same limits to it, as before.






Scaling to comparisons readers care about
Nobody plans in single seasons of a TV show or single thousands of dollars. Scale the coefficient to the step a reader cares about: fitted change = coefficient × number of unit steps, holding the other included predictors fixed. This resolves the Mentimeter question posed before the break.

Example 21.1 (Worked example: five seasons, half a million dollars, ten words) Holding the other included predictors fixed in equity_model:

Five later seasons: \(5\times(-0.836)=-4.18\) fitted equity percentage points.
$500,000 more requested: \(500{,}000/1{,}000 = 500\) units of ask_1k, so \(500\times(-0.0029)=-1.45\) fitted percentage points.
Ten additional description words: \(10\times(-0.128)=-1.28\) fitted percentage points — with the reminder that this coefficient is not significantly different from zero, so the scaled version is not either.

Rescaling a predictor changes the numerical coefficient and its SE by the same factor, but not the fitted values, t statistic, or substantive relationship. A “per dollar” coefficient of \(-0.0000029\) would be correct and unreadable; per $1,000 is readable on the data’s scale; per $100,000 is often the best unit for a sentence.







Try it: three seasons later and $200,000 more





In class this is the pair task. Two pitches are identical in description length; one is three seasons later and requests $200,000 more. Complete the steps before opening the answer.
Step 1 (given). Three seasons contribute \(3\times(-0.836)\) fitted percentage points.
Step 2 (you). Convert $200,000 into ask_1k units and multiply by the ask_1k coefficient.
Step 3 (you). Add the two contributions — the model is additive — and state the combined fitted difference in one protocol-complete sentence.






Check your answer





\(200{,}000/1{,}000=200\) units, so the request contributes \(200\times(-0.0029)\approx-0.58\). Combined: \(3(-0.836)+200(-0.0029)\approx-2.51-0.58=-3.09\) percentage points. Sentence: among the recorded pitches, a pitch three seasons later that requests $200,000 more is fitted to offer about 3.1 percentage points less initial equity, holding description length fixed — an association, not an effect.

b <- coef(equity_model)
3 * b["season"] + 200 * b["ask_1k"]

   season 
-3.087963 










What controls can and cannot do
Including a control can:

make a comparison more like-for-like on measured dimensions;
reduce residual variation, tightening intervals;
reveal that a simple association was partly compositional;
increase uncertainty when predictors overlap strongly.

Including a control cannot:

adjust for unmeasured factors;
fix reverse causality;
repair selection into the sample;
remove measurement error.

A “control variable” is just an included predictor. Nothing about the word control grants it a causal role; only a research design can do that.






Check: which of these four problems does adding ask_1k address?






later pitches request different amounts; (b) founder experience is not recorded; (c) equity offers may influence how much is asked; (d) only pitches that reached broadcast are in the file.

Only (a). It is a measured compositional difference, and holding ask_1k fixed removes it from the season comparison. Problems (b), (c), and (d) are unmeasured confounding, reverse causality, and sample selection — none of them touched by adding a measured control.





Assumptions extend to the full predictor set
For multiple regression, the Lecture 2 assumption list applies to the whole set of included predictors:

the conditional mean is linear in the included terms;
\(E[\varepsilon_i\mid X_{i1},\ldots,X_{ik}]=0\) — zero conditional mean at every combination of predictor values;
observations are independent under the design;
no predictor is an exact linear combination of the others;
classical SEs require constant conditional error variance;
exact small-sample t/F inference uses conditional normality.

High correlation among predictors — collinearity — does not bias OLS by itself, but it makes individual coefficients unstable and imprecise: the data contain little information to separate overlapping predictors. Exact linear dependence is worse: the coefficients are then not identified at all, and R drops a term. Instability is a precision problem; exact dependence is a no-answer-exists problem.


A coefficient plot keeps units visible


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
equity_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)
ci <- confint(equity_model)[-1, , drop = FALSE]
term_labels <- c("Season", "Amount requested ($1,000s)",
                 "Description length (words)")
coef_df <- data.frame(
  term = factor(term_labels, levels = term_labels),
  estimate = coef(equity_model)[-1],
  lower = ci[, 1],
  upper = ci[, 2]
)

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
                  colour = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.7, fatten = 2.6) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.02, y = 3.35, label = "no change = 0",
           hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  labs(x = "Estimated change in equity offered (percentage points)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 21.2: Coefficient estimates from the three-predictor model with 95% confidence intervals. Each row uses a different predictor unit, so magnitudes are not comparable across rows without the units table.





Read Figure 21.2 with the standing five-step sequence:

Axes: rows are predictors; the horizontal axis is the estimated change in initial equity offered, in percentage points.
Units: each row’s estimate is per one unit of that predictor — per season, per $1,000, per word. The rows are not on a common scale.
Marks: a dot is the coefficient estimate; its horizontal line is the 95% confidence interval; the dashed line marks zero.
Pattern: season and requested amount sit clearly left of zero; the description-words interval crosses zero. The ask_1k row hugs the zero line only because its unit step ($1,000) is tiny — its t statistic is about \(-5\). Visual size on this plot is a unit artefact, not evidence strength.
Limits: intervals reflect model-based sampling uncertainty among these recorded pitches; they say nothing about causation or unmeasured variables.


What an adjusted coefficient can and cannot say
Every slope in equity_model is a model-based comparison among the 1,441 recorded pitches: fitted conditional means at fixed values of the included predictors. “Holding the other included predictors fixed” never extends to variables outside the model — maturity, revenue, founder experience, and editorial selection are all unheld. The stability of the season slope across specifications is informative about the measured controls only; it proves no absence of omitted-variable bias. Initial equity offered is an on-air opening position, not a completed investment, and none of these associations is a causal effect of time, money, or word count.



Answering the driving question
At the same requested amount (and description length), the season trend persists: about \(-0.836\) equity percentage points per season, versus \(-0.824\) unadjusted. The money story does not absorb the time story here — later pitches offer less equity even compared at the same ask. And neither story is causal: an unmeasured driver could still lie behind both, exactly as firm size did in the constructed example.
Next: We can now hold other predictors fixed — as long as they are numerical. But many of the most interesting business comparisons are categorical: channels, segments, team compositions. Lecture 5 shows how categories enter a regression correctly — dummy variables and a reference group chosen deliberately — and how to judge a whole set of category terms at once with the partial F-test, because individually insignificant dummies can still be jointly worth having.

title: Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 75 minutes.

Retrieval (10 minutes)

What phrase must appear in a multiple-regression slope interpretation?
Why can a coefficient change after another predictor is added?
What is the zero conditional mean assumption?
Why do controls not automatically identify causality?
What problem can strongly overlapping predictors create?
What five elements belong in a slope interpretation?







Check your answers






“Holding the other included predictors fixed.”
The simpler slope may absorb relationships involving omitted correlated predictors; the added predictor takes back its share.
The error has mean zero at every combination of included predictor values.
Unmeasured confounding, selection, reverse causality, and measurement error can all remain after adjustment.
Unstable, imprecise individual coefficient estimates; exact overlap makes the model unidentified.
Estimate and direction, predictor step and unit, outcome unit, held-fixed predictors, and the sample/causal scope.






Practice (30 minutes)
Items 1–5 are unassisted checks of the core skills. Items 6–9 form the faded-to-unassisted ladder: item 6 repeats a calculation worked in class, items 7–8 change the numbers, and item 9 is the combined contrast you met half-finished in the pair task — now do it start to finish.

Interpret all three slopes from equity_model with units and conditioning.
Calculate 95% confidence intervals with confint(equity_model).
Test each coefficient against zero and distinguish three individual tests from one joint model test.
Remove description_words. Compare the season and request coefficients with the full model’s.
Name one plausible omitted variable and explain which model assumption it could threaten.
Interpret a five-season difference using the fitted season coefficient.
Interpret a $500,000 difference in requested amount.
Interpret a ten-word difference in description length and use its 95% interval to assess \(H_0:\beta=0\).
Compare two otherwise identical fitted pitches when one is three seasons later and requests $200,000 more. Calculate the combined fitted difference.







Check your answers






Holding the other two predictors fixed, among the recorded pitches: one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less initial equity; an additional $1,000 requested with about 0.0029 percentage points less (0.29 per $100,000); one additional description word with about 0.128 percentage points less.
The season interval is approximately \((-0.936, -0.736)\), the ask_1k interval \((-0.0040, -0.0018)\), and the description interval \((-0.351, 0.095)\).
Individual t-tests evaluate one \(\beta_j=0\) at a time; the overall F-test (F \(\approx\) 110.6 on 3 and 1437 df) evaluates all slope coefficients jointly.
Without description_words, the season coefficient is about \(-0.814\) and the ask_1k coefficient about \(-0.0029\). They change only slightly here; that empirical stability does not prove absence of omitted-variable bias.
Examples include venture maturity, revenue, founder experience, or editing decisions; if related to both an included predictor and offered equity, the omitted variable violates zero conditional mean.
Holding request and description length fixed, a pitch five seasons later is fitted to offer about \(5(-0.836)=-4.18\) equity percentage points less.
$500,000 equals 500 ask_1k units. Holding season and description length fixed, the fitted difference is \(500\times(-0.0029)\approx-1.45\) percentage points.
Ten words correspond to about \(-1.28\) fitted percentage points, holding season and request fixed. Multiplying the interval by 10 gives approximately \((-3.51, 0.95)\); because zero remains plausible, the two-sided 5% test does not reject a zero coefficient.
The fitted difference is \(3(-0.836)+200(-0.0029)\approx-3.09\) percentage points, holding description length fixed. Coefficient contributions add because the model is additive.






Cumulative mini-task (10 minutes)
Write one paragraph connecting the Lecture 2 diagnostics to equity_model: which residual checks would you run on this three-predictor fit, what would each look for, and what would you do about a highly influential pitch if you found one?






Check a model answer





A residuals-versus-fitted plot checks that the conditional mean is roughly linear in the included terms and that spread is roughly constant; curvature would question assumption 1, a funnel shape would question the classical SEs. Standardised residuals (rstandard) flag pitches the model fits unusually badly, and Cook’s distance flags pitches that individually move the coefficients. A flagged pitch — say, an extreme requested amount — gets investigated, not deleted: check the recorded values, refit with and without it, and report both fits if they disagree. Silent deletion is never an option.





Spaced review: one item from Lecture 3 (5 minutes)
For the simple model equity_offered_pct ~ season, the slope’s t statistic is about \(-17.34\). What is the overall F statistic of this one-predictor model, and why?






Check your answer





\(F = t^2 \approx 300.7\). With a single slope, the overall F-test and the two-sided t-test of that slope test the same hypothesis, and F is exactly the square of t. With several predictors that equivalence disappears — which is why Lecture 5 needs a genuine joint test.





Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question. A summary table reports, for the three-predictor model, season  -0.836  (SE 0.051) and description_words  -0.128  (SE 0.114). A student writes: “Season matters and word count does not, so descriptions have no effect on equity.” Give two corrections in the mock-exam Q4 style.






Check a model answer





First, “no effect” misreads non-significance: the interval \((-0.351, 0.095)\) contains zero and values near \(-0.35\), so the data are consistent with no association and with a modest negative one — not significant is not zero. Second, “effect” claims causation; both estimates are associations among recorded pitches, holding the other included predictors fixed, with no design that identifies a causal effect.





From the reading ladder (10 minutes)
Next rung of the reading ladder: open Zhao, Seibert & Hills (2005) via the university library and find the table predicting entrepreneurial intentions. Identify the outcome, the predictors of substantive interest, and the variables included as controls. Pick one coefficient and write the full protocol sentence — including “holding the other included predictors fixed” and the sample scope. Then name one variable not in the model that could drive both the predictor and the outcome, exactly like the constructed demonstration from today’s lecture.






Check your approach





Any defensible answer names the model-based nature of the comparison (no claim that identical students exist), keeps the units or scale of the predictor visible, and proposes an omitted variable with a plausible path to both sides — family business background, access to capital, and general self-confidence are all fair candidates. If your sentence could be read as causal advice (“increase X to raise intentions”), tighten it.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture — or any business you know well. Name one outcome you care about and two of its drivers that are correlated with each other (say, price and quality tier, or marketing spend and firm age), and write two sentences: which comparison would a regression of the outcome on only one driver mix together, and what would “holding the other fixed” let you see? There is no wrong answer; the point is spotting the confound in a business you actually know.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “Outcome: weekly orders; drivers: price and quality tier, which move together because premium boxes cost more. Orders-on-price alone would mix cheaper with lower-tier; holding tier fixed shows what a price cut does within a tier — the number I actually control.”



You can discuss this task — and any other task in this chapter — with Tilly, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to propose an omitted variable for your venture’s regression and challenge you to say whether a measured control could fix it.

Continue to Lecture 5: Categories as predictors and joint tests.
Formula sheet: Lecture 4 formulas.
For a more formal treatment, see James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Sections 3.2 and 3.3.3, and Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapter 20.

title: Lecture 5: Categories as predictors and joint tests
text:
Before class
Total preparation time: about 25 minutes.
Reactivate and predict (5 minutes). With three categories — all_men, all_women, and mixed — how many dummy variables does a model with an intercept need? Commit to a number, then answer the one-click Mentimeter question posted on Canvas: at the same season and requested amount, do you expect all-women teams to offer more, less, or about the same equity as all-men teams? The lecture resolves both.
R warm-up (10 minutes). Class starts from the subset and factor you build here — there are no hidden objects, so this warm-up is the setup. Bring the contrasts table:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000
levels(known_gender$gender)
contrasts(known_gender$gender)
If indicators and reference categories are unfamiliar, review Mathematics Refresher: indicators and reference categories.
